speakeroldname: Hon. Mr. STEVENS (Acting Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Customs and Excise; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Minister of Trade and Commerce; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: HOll-327J SURRENDER OF LANDS AGREEMENT WITH HUDSON'S BAY COMPANY
speechtext:
On the 23rd December, 1924, an agreement was entered into with the Hudson's Bay Company under which all lands held by the company within Forest reserves, Dominion parks and Indian reserves in the Fertile Belt were surrendered in exchange for vacant and available Dominion lands in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, to be selected by the company.
Clause one of the agreement reads as follows:
1.	The company agrees to surrender and release unto His Majesty all lands situate within Forest reserves, Dominion parks and Indian reserves in the Fertile Belt as defined in the said deed of surrender, hereinafter called the deed, and by an order in council P.C, 1667, bearing date the seventh day of May, 1896, to which the company holds title, and also any other interest, if any, in or to lands in the said reserves and parks to which it is entitled or claims to be entitled under the terms of the deed and the said legislation, in exchange for a quantity of vacant available Dominion lands in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, situate outside the said reserves and parks to be selected by the company, and equal in area to the sum of the following:
(a)	One-twentieth of the area of any land surveyed or unsurveyed included in Fertile Belt forest reserves other than the parks and reserves mentioned in subparagraph (c) hereunder. Forest reserves being as defined by the schedule to chapter 13 of the statutes 13 and 14 George V (Dom. 1923).
(b)	One-twentieth of the area of any land included prior to said enactment in Forest reserves other than those mentioned in said subparagraph (c).
(c)	The area of any land within Rocky Mountain park, Waterton Lake park, Rocky Mountain forest reserve and Indian reserves, unencumbered title to which is surrendered by the company to His Majesty.
Provided that no lands in Indian reserves and the Rocky Mountains forest reserve, the Rocky Mountains park or in the Waterton Lakes park as defined and shown on the homestead map or plan, Western Canada, of the Department of the Interior, seventeenth
Questions

edition, published in the year 1921, copy of which is hereto annexed, except lands to which ihe company surrendered, or surrenders, the unencumbered title in fee simple shall be credited to the company in the said exchange of lands. Provided that in cases where the company has leased mineral rights the lands shall be conveyed and the leases assigned to His Majesty, and the title shall be treated as an unencumbered title in fee simple for the purposes of this agreement. Provided that any lands heretofore granted or conveyed by His Majesty to the company for purposes of exchange in excess of the area heretofore relinquished or surrendered by the company for such exchange shall be reckoned and taken as lands selected and acquired by the company in satisfaction-pro tanto-of the company's rights to lands under this clause.
No other agreement has been entered into whereby the company agrees to abandon lands in Alberta for the privilege of choosing the same area in Manitoba or Saskatchewan.

PRIVILEGE-Mr. McMILLAN
On the Orders of the Day:

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question
of privilege. In yesterday's Mail and Empire I find the following:
Ottawa, Ontario, June 28.-The reasons Thomas McMillan, South Huron, was not entitled to a pair are stated in the following statement made by W. A. Boys, chief Conservative whip. Mr. Boys has given the following details of the situation over the McMillan pair.
When the Liberal whip asked me for a pair for Mr. McMillan, I refused on three grounds:
1.	Early in the session when Mr. A. D. Chaplin was sick in bed in Chatham and could not attend, I was refused a pair for him.
2.	Mr. McMillan had but a few days ago paired with Mr. Jones of New Brunswick, and had disregarded his pair and had voted.
3.	Mr. Carmichael, one of the Progressives, was supporting the opposition, so I was given to understand, and hod to leave for the west on account of the illness of -his daughter, and I felt his vote would offset Mr. McMillan's, and the actual voting strength of the House would thus be preserved.
In addition to the above reasons I since learned from Mr. Hocken that about five weeks ago Mr. McMillan had approached him for a sessional pair, to which Mr. Hocken had verbally agreed. On the 13th June, Mr. Hocken took sick and was confined to bed. On the 15th June, Mr. Hocken, owing to the unusual importance of the division, asked to have the pair confirmed by the Liberal whip, and asked Mr. McMillan to come to see him in his room. This [DOT] Mr. McMillan refused to do, and in consequence Mr. Hocken had to be carried into the House at two a.m., when he should have been at home in bed.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take exception to such a statement. So far as I am implicated, there is no truth in this statement. The hon. member for Royal (Mr. Jones) came to me and asked for a pair. My reply was: "All right, but I will do nothing myself; we will go to our whip, Mr. Casgrain," which we did.
I told Mr. Casgrain in the presence of Mr. Jones that he would like to pair with me, and while I was not going home till to-morrow, Friday, night, yet I would pair with him from that moment until my return on Monday night, but it was between the two of them. When the hon. member for Royal did return, he came to me and said that while he thought he was paired, he knew there was no blame attached to me.
As to the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr, Hocken), while we did meet and I would have liked a sessional pair, I got no such assurance from him, and considered our pair only temporary over the week end until our return on the following Monday. Furthermore, I know nothing of the hon. member for Toronto West Centre wishing the Liberal whip to confirm my pair with him on the evening of June 15. This report is
the first I have heard of it. That was the same night on which my pair expired with Mr. Jones, and while a messenger did hand me a note from Mr. Hocken, saying he wished to see me in his room, it was just when the vote was called, and having no obligation to him, I returned the note saying I could not come at present. I did not know of his illness till afterwards.

speakeroldname: Mr. H. C. HOCKEN (Toronto West Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement made
by the chief whip of the Conservative party which has just been read by the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan) is absolutely accurate. The hon. member came to me of his own initiative, outside the door of my room upstairs, and suggested that he and I should pair for the session. The words he used were these: "When I am away you won't vote, and when you are away I won't vote." If that is not to be understood as a sessional pair between two hon. members of the House, then I would like to know what is.
As to the occasion upon which he voted, I was under the doctor's orders at the time under no circumstances to leave my bed. I endeavoured to get the assistant whip to confirm the sessional pair I had made with the hon. member for South Huron, and he came to me and said that he had gone to the hon. member for South Huron and said that he would like h'im to come and see me in my room upstairs so that I could go home to bed, but that the hon. member for South Huron had refused to do so. That is the substance, and pretty nearly the text, of the statement made by the whip, and I am here to say that that statement is correct.

Mr. Speaker,
I have listened to the statement made by the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan). On Thursday the 10th of June I passed a note across the floor to the hon. member for' Shelbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Hatfield) asking him to favour me with a pair from Friday until the next Wednesday. He returned the note and said that he was paired with the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis (Mr. Short) until his return. I spoke to our whip and he said: "Perhaps you could see Mr. McMillan." I crossed the floor to where Mr. McMillan was sitting, somewhere near his old seat before we changed sides, and I asked him if he would give me a pair until next Wednesday. He said, "Wait till I see my whip." He spoke to the whip of the Liberal party, and the whip beckoned me to come up and said: "You wish to pair with

speechtext:

speechtext: I have not had time to go into them thoroughly but there is only one change that I can discover, and I have discussed the matter with the chief commissioner, and it is to the effect that instead of having a board of arbitration as was decided by this House, any change in the valuation of the soldiers' land is now left to the Soldier Settlement Board itself, with the opportunity of appeal to the Exchequer Court of Canada. There was some idea, I believe, that this would impose too much work upon the Exchequer court. However, I had the matter looked into and as far as I can find after rather hurried examination there would not be so many appeals as to embarrass the Exchequer court. At the same time there is a condition in the bill permitting the Exchequer court to delegate that work if they will to some other agency such as a district judge or a county court judge. So far as I have been able to look into the matter, and I have done that as thoroughly as time would permit, the change is satisfactory to all concerned. I have inquired of some of those who took great interest in the soldier settlement question when it was up and I think the matter is satisfactory from our standpoint unless there should be objections from somebody else.

subtopic: SOLDIER SETTLEMENT ACT, 1919, AMENDMENT CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS

subtopic: SOLDIER SETTLEMENT ACT, 1919, AMENDMENT CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Apparently the strongest argument that can be advanced in favour of the changes .made in this bill by the other body is the claim that they have left it open for us to go back to the original bill as passed in this House. They have left it open to go back to the local tribunal, and the strongest argument advanced by the minister apparently, as to why we should accept their amendment, is that they have left open the door to get back to the bill as it passed this House; in other words, to the local tribunal. That was the provision in the bill as it left this chamber.
Then again the argument is used that appealing to the Exchequer court will provide uniformity and will be more reliable. That argument might apply were it a question of law, or a case where it was desirable to have a uniformity of law throughout Canada; but how can you have uniformity of judgment?

subtopic: SOLDIER SETTLEMENT ACT, 1919, AMENDMENT CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Order. I cannot hear a word.

subtopic: SOLDIER SETTLEMENT ACT, 1919, AMENDMENT CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
How can you have uniformity of judgment in the matter of the value of land which varies every five miles? It was alleged in the previous debate or possibly in the other chamber, that by having a judge, one man acting, he could make up his mind what the value was in a given case. Then the matter was settled. All he had to do was to adopt- that value in every case. To anyone who knows anything about the common sense view it is simply ridiculous, because the value of land varies, not only in every province, but every few miles. In one case it might cost $300 or $400 to clear land. That is common in the west. Is that condition to be compared with the case of broken land on the prairie where it does not require anything to clear it? The purpose of the bill was to see that justice would be done by the local tribunal in every local condition that arose. I think it would be desirable that we should have the full amendments of the bill before us, so that we would know what particular sections were affected and in what way. The amendments will be found in Votes and Pro-
ceedings. Perhaps in line 95 you strike out the word "and". It may not mean much or it may be very important. In one of the Senate Hansards I saw a suggestion made on the addition of a clause which while apparently innocent, might be used in a court directed to the strictly legal aspect for the purpose of upsetting the whole bill; because it said -it could only apply to those soldiers whose condition was such that it was impossible for them to continue with the overload of indebtedness which they might have. The wording of the clause was of such a character that it might be held, "Well here is this man with an overload of $2,000, but he is a hardworking industrious chap, with a wife and growing family. It is not impossible for them to survive that load and overcome it." That was not the principle of the bill as it left this House. The principle was that fair and evenhanded justice should be meted out, and the case should not be decided upon legal technicalities at all. At a later stage I saw that same bill in the Senate and I could not find that clause; but if that clause is in the measure it requires careful investigation. The minister should take steps before the hill comes up again to have the amendments printed in such a way as to show what their effect will be. If we have to wade through forty or fifty amendments, where we are told to strike out the word "or" and insert two or three words in another place, going through it in the hurried way in which we are doing, justice will not be done.

Sir HENRY DRAYTON (Leader of the House) moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 148, for the purpose of establishing in Canada a system of long term mortgage credit for farmers.

Long Term Farm Loans

What are
these amendments?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I desire to bring these amendments to the attention of hon. members. I think they have been tabled for some time and are available to hon. members who desire to look into the question.

Did the minister say
they had been tabled for some time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I think the information has been before us.
Yesterday.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I thought it
was earlier. They were tabled only yesterday, but the bill is a very important one, and I think we should consider it as 'early as possible. I propose to take up the amendments one by one and draw them to the attention of my hon. friends. The amendments appear in the Votes and Proceedings. The first amendment is one made to clause 3 of the bill. That clause provides for the appointment of the members of the board. I believe the House will agree that there is no objection whatever to that amendment; it simply adds, after the word "council" the words, "On such terms and conditions as the Governor in Council may prescribe."
What does that mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Personally I do not think it adds anything to it.
It makes no difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
It makes no difference. Generally when anyone is appointed he is appointed on such terms and conditions as the person making the appointment chooses to attach. That is all that is said. The amendments are to be found on page 497 of Votes and Proceedings. The amendment to section 5 merely makes it clear that the capital stock shall be based on the principal outstanding on mortgages from time to time rather than on the original face value of the mortgage. The first three and a half lines of subsection (a) of section 5 are struck out and it is provided instead that the government of Canada may subscribe an initial amount not exceeding $5,000,000 and pay that amount in such subscriptions and at such times as in the judgment of the board are necessary.
On page 3 after the word "total" the words "amount of principal outstanding on" are added. The effect is to restrict the capital to the amount actually outstanding. I do
not think there is any other change in that section except one providing that shares in the capital stock may be transferred at the option of the board where the sale of property is satisfactory to the board.
Next we come to section 7. On page 5 of the bill there is a charge of some moment. The matter was discussed in the House and there were some differences of opinion as to W'hether we were doing right or not. The particular provision had reference to the limitation of expenses of operation to one per cent of the loan, and after some discussion that was carried. I remember supporting it myself although other hon. gentlemen considered it unfair to fix such a limitation until it had been seen how matters worked out. It was thought that we could trust to the board to manage things properly. However, we put it in and the Senate struck it out. That limitation having been removed the matter is left entirely to the proper administration of the board. In his note on the section Mr. Finlayson, who had the matter in hand both in this House for the minister and in the Senate, says that it was felt that the judgment of the board should be unfettered in fixing upon the provision to be made in the mortgage interest rate to take care of cost of operation.
There is another change in subsection 6 of section 7. That subsection provides:
Every .farm loan shall be repayable in equal annual or semi-annual instalments of principal and interest.
The Senate has added the words "at the option of the borrower." No one I think will object to that. It simply means that the borrower can decide whether he wishes to have his loan carry payments annually or semi-annually.
In subsection 7 the words "all assessments and taxes" are struck out and the following words are substituted:
All assessments, taxes and other charges necessary to he paid for the security of the board in respect of the loan.
The amendment is to provide that the borrower shall pay, in addition to assessments and taxes, such other charges as may be found necessary for the protection of the board in relation to the upkeep of its property. Personally, I do not know exactly what was feared, but hon. gentlemen who live in the district will probably appreciate the reason for the change. At any rate, the amendment does not appear to be of considerable importance. The subsection as amended by the Senate reads:
(7) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Interest Act every borrower shall .pay simple interest
Long Term Farm Loans

on defaulted payments at a rate not exceeding eight per cent per annum and shall agree to pay when due all assessments, taxes and other charges necessary (to be paid for the security of the board in respect of the loan and to effect such insurance as the -board may require. Should such taxes, assessments and charges not be paid when due, they may be paid by the board and charged to the borrower, and if not repaid to the board on or before the next interest date with interest thereon at a rate not exceeding eight per cent per annum the borrower shall be considered in default under the mortgage.
The effect of this amendment is that if these payments have to be made by the board in the ordinary course the board may charge interest on such payments, not to exceed 8 per cent.
There is a change in subsection 8 of the same section. The amendment recognizes the right of the borrower to repay his Ipan in whole or in part at any time within the specified period.
At no time shall the borrower pay more than 8 per cent on the loan in arrears. Does that 8 per cent include all charges?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
It would cover all charges which have been actually paid by the board; that is all. Tlie rate is not fixed. That is something for the board to arrange in the ordinary way, but they cannot stipulate for a greater rate of interest than 8 per cent.
We were considering the section dealing with payments by borrowers. As I was pointing out, this subsection has been amended to recognize the right of the borrower to repay his loan in whole or in part at any time without notice, instead of after five years as in the original bill. This privilege, however, will be subject to regulations not inconsistent with the Interest Act, which provides that the penalty for repayment without notice after five years' duration shall not exceed a bonus of three months' interest. As I said to my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Dunning) I would think this would be a matter of administration.	.
I said so when the bill was going through this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I would think
the board ought to take the money at any time without any trouble at all. This is to help the borrower because before he had not the right to repay without notice, This helps him to the extent that he can repay at any time without waiting five years, but that he may be charged a bonus of not more than three months interest. In my view, when we establish the machinery of administration the proper way of dealing with this would be

to have a rule enabling a man to repay his loan at any time without charging him any bonus whatever.

Before my hon. friend leaves section
8, may I direct his attention, if it is permis- [DOT] sible, to certain suggested amendments that were made in another House by the leader of the government. A resolution was presented there and seconded by an hon. gentleman who is mentioned as a member of this government. I should like to know what my hon. friend's attitude is in that regard. I observe some hon. gentleman over there said that if you were going to chloroform the bill you might as well chloroform it at once. I submit to my hon. friend that even should the bill pass this House, if the government is not sympathetic towards it there will be means of tying it up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Some amendments were proposed in the other House but were withdrawn; for example, an amendment to the effect that this law was not to be operative without the consent of the provinces, as I recall it. We are not receiving this bill in any such spirit at all. So far as we have gone with these amendments, I have not seen anything which really tends to injure the administration of this bill one way or the other. I do not know if my hon. friends are going to say we will strike something later on of that character, but so far we have not.
I quite admit to my hon. friend that the usefulness of all legislation depends upon how it is carried out-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
-and I hope
this bill is going to be properly carried out. So far as I am concerned, it will be properly carried out.
I congratulate my hon. friend upon his rapid conversion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I am quite delighted to give my hon. friend an opportunity of exchanging smiles with me, but he is entirely wrong. Why, we were calling for this provision before the bill was brought down.
If my hon. friend will go back a little he will remember the ghost of a bill we had last year, and he will remember that the then opposition laid down the lines of a bill which my hon. friend afterwards put the clothes on.
I congratulate him on that.
Sections 9 and 10 are pretty well tied together. They speak for themselves. The calling of the loan is to be at the option of the board. I do not think there is any difficulty about that. Then comes section 8, in

Long Term Farm Loans
which a change is made in the number of members to act as agents for the provincial board. The number of members is reduced from five to four, the reduction being in the members representative of the borrowers from two to one. There is also a proviso-
I am giving the effect of the whole thing- that until such time as in the judgment of the board nomination by the borrower is practicable, all the functions of the provincial board may be exercised by the three members nominated by the government of the province. I think my hon. friend will say that that is all right.

No, Mr. Speaker, I am not altogether certain that it is all right, but I doubt if at this stage we can do anything to remedy it. As my hon. friend well knows, one of the major principles underlying this bill was that it should ultimately develop into that type of credit control which would allow the borrowers themselves to administer their own credit. I remember the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) supported us strongly on that point before the Banking committee in the last four years. The ideal condition is an agricultural credit system which will in the ultimate rest absolutely in the hands of the borrowers and be administered by them. This amendment to a great extent delays that action. We need more representation. You have to encourage the borrowers to take an interest in this matter and the best way to arouse their interest is by giving them power to elect their representatives to the board. This amendment cuts down their representation from two to one. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I do not think we can do anything at this late stage with respect to this feature, but I simply wish to go on record as intimating to the administration that unquestionably in future we, or others, will come back to this House asking that recognition be given to the borrowers' interest in the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The next section to be amended is number 9, where the word, "stock" is put in after "capital". I need not pause there at all, for it is just carrying out the purpose of the first amendment that I drew attention to. Then we have subsection 5 of section 9:
If as a result of proceedings under any mortgage the title to the property securing such mortgage is transferred to the board, the stock held by the borrower in the board shall be cancelled and the amount paid thereon by the borrower shall be forfeited to the board.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Regina): I do not know whether we are exactly in order
in discussing the amendments in this manner, but, Mr. Speaker, I object to the amendment.
I do not think it is fair to the borrower. His land is forfeited to the board, and in addition the amount of his stock, which, remember, he paid for in cash, and which was equivalent to 5 per cent of the original amount of his mortgage, is also forfeited to the board. It is not even credited to him in any manner as part of his debt. It is true there may very well be circumstances where the amount owing to the board by the mortgagor may be so much greater than the value of the stock which the board takes over as to involve the taking also of the borrower's interest in the association equivalent, as I have said, to 5 per cent of the amount of his loan. But surely we should not assume that all cases will be of that kind. Under the amendment, however, as suggested by the Senate, all cases would be treated alike, and whatever the situation of the borrower and his security might be he would nevertheless forfeit the 5 per cent interest in the capital stock of the institution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I speak subject to correction by my hon. friend, whose bill this very largely is. I would have thought that if it is not clear it ought. to be made clear, and as a matter of administration it must be made clear, that so far as that stock i3 concerned it must be looked upon as a payment pro tanto on the borrower's debt.
What is "pro tanto?"

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: "To the extent it goes." You see, the man is given a certain amount of stock.	* '
It is a partial security.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes, which is
held by those administering it, and I submit that no board would ever think of taking that stock and the property as well if, by taking any of the stock, the debt would be paid.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
speechtext:
If the debt would be more than
paid it would be highly immoral.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
And I do not
think that is at all the intent of the section.

That is the language.
- Mr. G. G. COOTE (Macleod): Could not further words be added to that amendment, that it should apply on the mortgage?

It is only in the case of
one particular proceeding, when the board have failed to realize on a mortgage security sufficient to pay the mortgage debt, and of
Long Term Farm Loans

course I think it would be highly immoral indeed if, when a transfer of the mortgaged property, plus -the stock, was more than sufficient to liquidate the actual indebtedness outstanding, the board appropriated that excess.

If that is
the spirit in which the act will be administered it will be satisfactory, but it should be made very clear that in the event of a delay in the realization of a security, if the amount of money secured including the 5 per cent is more than enough to pay the mortgagor's liability, then there should be a refund.
It seems to me, at this late hour, that that could be arranged by regulation, but it should be clearly understood as my hon. friend has pronounced it.
If the Acting Minister of Finance, whoever is acting at the moment-I am really at a loss to know.
It is all the same.

Yes, it is
all the same. If whoever is acting will go on record that a regulation will be enacted providing that the spirit enunciated here will be incorporated in the bill, it will be satisfactory.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
There is not
the slightest difficulty in that. Furthermore, before any proceedings would be taken the man must be credited with the amount of the stock.

In an
important matter like this why should not, the procedure be incorporated in the bill, without trusting to some regulations which are to come afterward? I strongly protest against legislation going through in this fashion. These things should be printed and submitted to the House, and there should be no cross-firing here unless we know what we are doing. I want to go on record as saying that this manner of doing business is entirely improper, in my judgment, and should not be carried on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I am afraid my hon. friend is singularly ignorant of the business of the House. If he will look at the Votes and Proceedings he will find everything before him, and I have no doubt he can read as well as anyone. If hon. gentlemen want to delay this bill and tie it up the responsibility must be theirs. I am willing to assist in every possible way in providing the fullest measure of relief to farmers all over Canada under this measure. That is my desire, but if for technicalities or the like we are 
to be held up certainly the fault is not ours. This bill will have to go back to the Senate if any further changes are made. I am perfectly willing to accept what has been said by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) to the fullest possible extent, and I really think the House should take the same stand. However, I am entirely in the hands of the House.
Go on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Very well. There is a new clause A, having to do with the audit of the books. It is as follows:
An audit of the books of the board and of each provincial board shall be made in accordance with regulations made under the provisions of section sixteen of this act by a firm of charterd accountants appointed for that purpose by the Governor in Council, and a copy of the report of the said accountants on the annual statement of the board shall be laid before parliament by the minister within the first fifteen days of the first session thereof following the date of the said report.
I do not think my hon. friend will object to that.
Not at -all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the spectacle that we are witnessing to-day shows how the course of events has proved that we were perfectly right. We have opposite a so-called government representing, according to our constitution, absolutely nothing at all. We have the leader of the House (Sir Henry Drayton) telling U3 from his seat in this House that he really does not reprent a government, but a government to be named later. The situation is absurd; it is ridiculous, and the people of Canada will not stand for it. Notwithstanding the efforts of hon. gentlemen on the other side, efforts which are in some measure published, and efforts which are in a greater measure to be hidden, we know what has been going on; we know the methods adopted by the other side to get into the position in which they are to-day, and the public of this country is entitled to know the true story of the events of this week.
Are we as members of this House realizing our responsibilities? The leader of the House requests us to forget everything which was said this session in order to give a chance to the Tories to organize for the next election, which they will bring on in the fall. Are we, in order to help the Conservative party to put through their policy of protection, to abandon every principle which has been voiced in this House during this session and in former sessions? Are we, Mr. Speaker, because the leader of the House, or the supposed leader of the House, the representative of this embryo government, asks us to go home in order that they shall be rid of 
their troubles-are we going to listen to them and refuse to vote according to our principles on this very important question?
I address myself now particularly to the western representatives in this House. This government will either carry on or ask for a dissolution; there is no other course. If they are to carry on as they have pledged themselves to do, how wil they carry on? Will they change their policy? Is any man on the other side willing to get up at this stage of the debate and inform the House that the Conservative party have changed their policy on the tariff question? Will any man with authority get up in this House and give an assurance to the representatives of the western provinces or to the representatives of the eastern provinces that there has been any alteration in their tariff principles, or supposed principles? These gentlemen were either sincere when they spoke on tariff questions in the course of this session, or they were not. If they were sincere, there is not one man in the House who is in favour of a low tariff who can support them for a minute. There is not one man who through any process of mental activity could reach the conclusion that he can support these people if they are sincere in their tariff policy as they have announced it. If they were not sincere in stating their policy, that is a further and a stronger reason to put them out immediately.

My hon. friend tells me to go ahead, and I know why he says that. Here is a gentleman who has been a judge on a moral question, who would put us out of power because we were not worthy of running this country. I am perfectly willing to discuss moral questions with him at any time anywhere, but I do not think it will be to his advantage, and he knows it.
This fight, Mr. Speaker, is only beginning.-If there are members of this House who are under the impression that this shadow government is going to be allowed to run this country without our fighting, they are making a mistake. If the leader of the House is under the impression that by smiling away as he did this afternoon and asking us to pass legislation which was opposed by gentlemen on the other side all through the session, he will attain the one object his party have in mind, that is, the taking hold of the administration of public affairs in this country and putting through their policy, he is making a mistake. We are doing what we think is our duty, and we appeal to every member of this House to consider with great care the resolution which is now before the Chair. This resolution is of paramount importance, and no member can escape giving his opinion before the great tribunal, the people of this country, is appealed to. The eyes of Canada are upon this House, and now is the time for every member to show his sincerity. Now is the time for every member to state in no uncertain way where he stands, and I am very anxious to have the vote recorded on this question.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think on an occasion of this kind, when a change of administration) has taken place it is well that an announcement of the policy of the new administration should be given to this House and to the people of the country as early as possible. My reasons for saying that are many, and I think they are valid 'and weighty reasons. I am pleased to give my support to this motion moved by -the right hon. leader of the opposition which reads as follows:
That in the opinion of this House the fiscal policy of the government, as enunciated by the present Prime Minister when leader of His Majesty's opposition would prove detrimental to the country's continued prosperity and prejudicial to national unity.
Among the reasons I have for coming to that conclusion are the following: During the last campaign which preceded the general election statements were made by the present Prime Minister and by many of his acting (ministers as to their attitude on the tariff
issue. I am not going to quote them at length. I will not take up the time of the House by doing so. But I have before me part of a newspaper report of a meeting at Fort William on September 29, which was addressed by the then leader of the opposition, the present Prime Minister. The report goes on to say:
Dr. Manion, the Fort William candidate, and W. F. Langworthy, Conservative candidate in Port Arthur, also spoke at both meetings. They discussed local problems and urged the necessity for a higher protective tariff, quoting examples from local conditions.
I find that later on in this House the hon. member for Port William, who is now Acting Postmaster General, told us-I am not absolutely clear as to his actual words but the intention was unmistakable-that the tariff was a ruinous one to Canada, that the low tariff was ruining this country. He mentioned the tariff on automobiles and stated that it was lower than the tariff in any other country in the world where these vehicles are being manufactured. The hon. gentleman told us that he knew of no act of the then government that was tending to improve the condition of the people of Canada. *

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
I shall be very
glad to accede to my hon. friend's request and speak a little louder. I submit that in view of the statement referred to by the hon. member for Fort William the present administration will have to repeal all the acts passed by its predecessors for the purpose of benefiting the people of Canada.
We were also told by the Acting Postmaster General on April 20 that no industrial leader dare invest his money in Canada today. We were told many other things about
Supply-Fiscal Policy

the tariff, including the statement that in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec two million farmers are selling their products to the industrial workers in those provinces and so getting a great deal of benefit from a protective tariff. I have no idea where the hon. gentleman got his figures that there were two million farmers in these two provinces, but the opinion of the farmers of Ontario and Quebec, as well as of the other provinces, as expressed by them on many occasions, is that a high protective tariff is not conducive to their welfare.
Another statement made by the Acting Postmaster General was that free trade and a lower tariff had ruined the farmers of Great Britain and forced them off the land. I want to assure my hon. friend that it was not free trade and a lower tariff that ruined the farmers of Great Britain but Tory landlordism plus the high tolls which the absentee rent collectors charged up against the land- as high as the land would bear-not to speak of the high tariff that was enforced prior to 1846, and the competition for land engaged in after that date and leased by absentee landlords in' many cases. We were further advised by hon. members opposite that the people of Canada should endeavour to build up their cities at the present time in order to secure a larger market for the products of the farms. I leave it to the imagination of any hon. members of this House to conceive if the time can possibly come within their own span of life when the people of Canada will be able to build cities sufficiently large and populate them to the extent required to consume the products of all the farms of the country. It is like another remedy that was proposed during the general elections by the then leader of the opposition, the present Prime Minister. He told the people of the Maritime provinces that his policy for remedying the grievances under which they suffered was to pay part of the cost of the freight on the products they raised in order to secure an entry for those products into the central markets of Ontario and Quebec, and that that policy would apply to the products of the western provinces as well-that in the case of the western provinces also he would be in favour of paying part of the freight on their products into the central markets of Ontario and Quebec. It would require a very vivid imagination indeed to see where the products of the Maritime provinces-such as lumber, fruit, poultry, beef, butter, and fish from the sea-could find an adequate market in the protected cities of the central provinces by securing lower freight 
rates, or where the farmer of western Canada could secure such a market for his livestock, his grain products, and his dairy products in the same provinces. That they could secure such a market by simply reducing the freight rates is absolutely unreasonable and out of the question and yet we are asked to believe that is the policy hon. gentlemen opposite would carry out as a set-off to high [DOT]protection on manufactured goods.
The amendment of the right hon. leader of the opposition to-day goes on to say that the Conservative tariff policy would be prejudicial to national unity. As an illustration that such will foe its effect I need only quote from the headlines of papers published on October 18th last. Tor example one of these reads as follows:
Western farmer cartooned as "Carving alive struggling manufacturer, bound band and foot";
Then we find in the body of the article this statement:
While half a million is being spent on billboard advertising, proclaiming the virtues of higher protection, the offensive element does not appear in such places. Rather it is in the newspapers. In a recurrent series of cartoons, the dominant suggestion i6 that Premier Mackenzie King is under servility to the west.
In one of these productions the western fanner is pictured as carving alive a struggling manufacturer bound hand and foot, while Mackenzie King is looking on gleefully. In another it is Mr. King who is harnessed up, and a western farmer is shown with the reins cracking the whip over the leader.
What is being pictured in a way that is calculated to arouse prejudice against the King government and against the west is reflected also in the editorial columns of the press and in the speeches of Conservative leaders.
If the publication of news of that kind is necessary in order to secure higher tariff conditions in Canada, it is needless to say that the people of western Canada are not very strong for a higher tariff. But as to the effect of such statements on national unity there can be no question in the world that they are bound to work ill to the Dominion as a whole. I should like to contrast some of the things that have been said by the present Prime Minister and his acting ministers and supporters in this House with what a former great leader of the Conservative party had to say, and the principles in which ]he believed, in regard to tariff matters. Sir Robert Giffen, in his article on taxation an the Encyclopaedia Britannica says:
"Sir John A. Macdonald, the great protectionist Prime Minister of Canada, in a conversation with the present writer in 1882, avowed without hesitation that protectionist taxation in Canada was indefensible on economic grounds, and he defended it exclusively for political reasons."

Sup-ply-Fiscal Policy
That is not the attitude that our friends of the Conservative party have been taking for the past six months in the House and for the past few years throughout the country.
In the national policy resolution introduced into parliament by Sir John. A. Macdonald on March 12, 1878, one of the reasons given for the adoption of a national policy of protection is that, "moving, as it ought to do, in the direction of a reciprocity of tariffs with our neighbours, so far as the varied interests of Canada may demand, (it) will greatly tend to procure for this country eventually a reciprocity of trade.''
I submit that Sir John A. Macdonald was more farseeing in1 his day than his successors have been at any time. In order that reciprocity in trade might be secured between ourselves and other countries, it might be politically defensible that a tariff should be arranged between the two countries on certain commodities. But that is not the way the tariff has been used in late years. The claim has often been made in this House during the present session that the United States was the greatest, the wealthiest and the most prosperous and up-to-date country in the world. To much of that I take no exception, but we were told something to which I seriously object, namely that Canada was in a forlorn, dependent and poverty-stricken condition. We were told by the late leader of the opposition, now acting Prime Minister, that we had entered upon a period of depression in 1921, along with every other nation on the continent, and that we had remained in that period of depression 'longer than any other nation. I do not think it is fair that the statement should go out from this House that Canada has been in a state of depression and has remained longer in that state of depression than any other nation. I do not know what he meant by saying any other nation on the continent, but I take it that he intended to include Mexico, Panama, Bolivia, and all the other South American republics. It is not fair to state that we have remained in that period of depression longer than any other country on the continent. I remember last fall reading the report of a meeting in Vancouver addressed by the hon. member who is now acting Minister of Customs; at least I assume it was he, because the report stated that Mr. H. H. Stevens addressed the meeting and stated that if Canada did not wake up and get rid' of Mackenzie King and his government, in the next three months, the country would be on the road to bankruptcy in, four years. At a time when the railroads, the banks and the commercial institutions were telling the people of Canada that they were enjoying prosperity such as they had not enjoyed for many years, this was the kind of service that
was being rendered to Canada by gentlemen who are part of the shadow government in office at Ottawa at the present time. I have in my hand a piece of literature which was used to considerable effect throughout the country. It is headed, "Land values and protection", and it is issued under the auspices of an organization which has an advisory council and an executive committee. I notice that the president of that executive committee was quoted by the hon. member for Toronto Northeast (Mr. Baker) as an up-to-date authority. This literature was used in the campaign and one statement reads:
We predicted in April, 1924, in our pamphlet "If Canada would prosper" that unless the tariff were raised our railroads would drift towards insolvency, and that this would react against the west. This is coming about much more rapidly than we anticipated.
We find that for the month of May past the net earnings of the Canadian National Railway were 706 per cent higher than a year ago. Under these conditions these prophets of evil told us that we were ruining Canada and driving our railroads into insolvency. That statement never was true. It is dangerous to prophesy unless you kn/ow what is going to happen.
For a few moments, I wish to look into the condition of the rich country to the south of us, with particular reference to tihie middle and western farming community. During the past few months, the condition of agriculture in the middle west and throughout the United States as a whole has caused grave concern to public men at Washington and leaders of public opinion elsewhere in that country. I hold in my hand an article written by Representative Dickinson, of Iowa, in which he says that the United States industrial structure is four-cornered. One corner, manufacturing, is protected by a .tariff wall, while another comer, .the railroads, is protected by the Interstate Commerce Commission which endeavours to see that the rates are so fixed as to give the railroads a .profit of 5 per oent. But some of them make much more than that. The third comer consists of labour, which is protected by the exclusion of immigration to that .country. But the fourth comer, represented by the farmers of the country, is not protected. That corner is extremely wobbly. There is nothing to hold it up. In the opinion of Mr. Dickinson, and in ithe opinion of the majority of the farmers in the middle west, there is no possible way in which a tariff prop can be placed under that fourth comer, and the only way to assure reasonable prosperity is that all the legs be knocked out of the structure, and that the structure be

I am
glad that this resolution is before the House, as I washed to have an opportunity to express my attitude with regard to the fiscal policy of this country. I was elected in opposition to the fiscal policy of the Right Hon. Arthur iMeighen and the Conservative party as a whole. I represent a district in Alberta. In our province the one great thing we are interested in is the production of agricultural products, the selling of the same and the buying of implements and supplies of every kind and description at as low a price as possible. That is the life of our country and the only condition in which our country can prosper is where the taxes or the tariff on the goods they must purchase in large quantities are lowered. I remember when the. Right Hon. Arthur Meighen was speaking in his tour of the west he told us that the reduction of freight rates westward for the relief of the west was utterly unjustifiable, or "utterly indefensible," to use his exact words, and I made up my mind that I would go out before the people, and if the people elected me I would protest in parliament to the best of my ability, in the interests of the provinces of the west and therefore of all of Canada, against higher tariffs. If we help the western provinces we help all of Canada. I listened for three or four months to the speeches of the members of the then opposition, now on the government side, and they said. "We are losing money on grain shipped eastward. If the Crowsnest pass agreement were not in operation we could collect thirty millions more from the farmers of the west," and their policy was, "No more statutory freight rates." The people of western Canada must have reasonable freight rates, and we wish to put ourselves on record on 'this matter. Hon. members say, "We cannot do anything without the consent of parliament." I say we do not want to build up a party or organization which talks that kind of propaganda, and has such a fiscal policy. I want to go back to my constituency as having recorded my opposition to that policy. That is the attitude I took when I was elected and that is the attitude I take now'.
The government just retired met parliament in January and in sportsmanlike fashion they consulted the House on the question as to who should be Prime Minister. Parliament

decided by a majority that the right hon. gentleman now in opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) should be Prime Minister, and hon. members opposite refused at that time to grant an adjournment so that he might get his cabinet constituted. They voted supply piecemeal and generally did all that they could to embarrass the government. Now they want us to help them along. The late government brought down a budget which met with the approval of the Canadian people and they carried out the programme they outlined in the Speech from the Throne, including rural credits, which the people wanted, the West India treaty, and amendments to the Grain Act. The Tariff Advisory Board has also been appointed and the commission to inquire into Maritime rights has been set up. The question of freight rates is also being looked into. These are all matters in which the people are vitally interested and they were all undertaken by the late government.
I protest against the fiscal policy which the party opposite has advocated both in this House and in the country. Hon. gentlemen opposite told the government at the opening of the session that it could not function owing to the number of vacancies in the cabinet. To-day there is nothing but vacancies in the government which is attempting to conduct the business of the country. I do not want to prolong this debate, but I must decline to vote confidence in hon. gentlemen opposite unless they are prepared to assure this House that they stand for a different fiscal policy. This assurance they will not give us, and for that reason I must support the motion which has been brought forward.

In this particular instance the difficulty is even greater owing to the peculiar circumstances that surround the discussion. Personally I am not very much in favour of what might be termed "blocking tactics," motions intended simply to harass the government. Whichever party may be in power, I believe the government ought to be given a fair chance. From the standpoint of some of us, who, notwithstanding what some hon. gentlemen in this House may say, still regard ourselves as independent, and who have nothing to gain immediately

from party conflict, I do not think there is any reason at any stage for lending ourselves to any blocking of the business of the House.
I must observe however that I cannot be blind to the fact that the present government is in power through no act of this House. I am not a constitutional authority, but from what little I have read I 'have always understood that in accordance with British practice the king should 'be advised by his ministers and should obey their voice. I do not see why British practice should be departed from in Canada. I recognize that all along Canada has been in a position somewhat different from that of Great Britain. Hon. gentlemen opposite have told us again and again, when we have referred to the necessity for defining our status in this country, that it was quite unnecessary to do so inasmuch as undoubtedly we had autonomy in Ganad'a. They have 'assured us that we were equal with the Motherland in all respects. I would pass
directly then, Mr. Speaker, to the question of responsibility, and here again, not being well versed in constitutional law, I confess that I am a little bit puzzled to know just how the Acting Prime Minister, or the gentleman who here to-day acts for the Prime Minister can accept responsibility under the circumstances. I do not understand it at all, and I would ask to have an explanation before very long from the government, from those members who know constitutional law, as to the constitutional principle under which, under these circumstances, the Prime Minister can claim to have responsibility for advising the Governor General.
The position that our group takes with regard to such matters, I will remind the House, is that there ought to be some way in which there could be condemnation of the government without such condemnation necessarily involving a change of government. I think we are just coming to the difficulty of which I tried to warn the House a week ago. May I quote, or give the substance at least, of my remarks on that occasion. I said:
I want to be clearly understood. We must insist upon being free to condemn certain actions of the government without necessarily replacing the government by any party or group in the House.
I went on to point out:
Now government has to do with a great variety of subjects; government policy covens a very wide field indeed. We have been spending, I suppose almost half the time of the House this session discussing the question of lower or higher tariffs. As I have said before, I do not believe that either free trade or protection or higher protection will solve the economic problems that face this countiy. But I would ask hon. members whether a great question such as free trade or protection, or higher ot lower protection, is to be set aside without consideration merely because a certain individual named Moses Aziz did something

Supply-Fiscal Policy

that was wrong, or because a minister in dealing with that case took an action which some do not regard as justifiable.
This is the position in which the House now finds itself. There has been a condemnation of the government. I do not think anyone will question that. The vote last night clearly showed condemnation of the government, but side by side with that, I would point out that such condemnation dealt with only one particular question, and we must remember that there is a great variety of questions which must be dealt with 'by a government, and this country has not decided, and this House has not decided, that it wishes the policies of hon. gentlemen opposite to prevail in this country. I had expected that there would be a statement of policy from the provisional government ; I think we were entitled to that. When parliament assembles it is customary for the government to give a statement of its policy in what is known as the Governor General's Speech. In that Speech the government of the day announces the general policy which it proposes to pursue. The policy that is being pursued at the present time presumably is that announced in the Governor General's Speech six months ago. Do hon. gentlemen opposite intend to follow out that policy? Are they prepared to follow it out to the limit? I submit, Mr. Speaker, that no other policy has been announced on the floor of this House. If hon. gentlemen opposite propose to carry out that policy in detail, sincerely and honestly, I would have to give them my support because I am not concerned primarily with the individuals who happen to be in office. But I want to know, and I have a right to know, whether they intend to carry out that policy. If they do not, then this House has a right to know what alternate policy they propose. I had expected a statement of the government's policy*-perhaps hardly immediately, since their leader is not in the House and they have had but a short time to prepare-but I would have expected a general statement, and since that has not been given it seems to me that gentlemen on this side of the House are justified in introducing motions of this character in order to draw out what is the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite.
In my speech in the recent debate a week ago I referred not merely to questions of the tariff, but to other questions-to our imperial relations, for instance. I am reminded that this fall we are holding an Imperial conference. Will any hon. gentleman in this House say that the group opposite has any mandate whatever from Canada or any right what-

ever to speak for Canada at that conference? The fact that certain Progressive members joined with the Conservatives in condemning laxity on the part of the government does not mean at all that the Conservative party has any right to go over to England and announce an Imperial policy which has not been before this House. I called attention, I notice, to other questions in which the country is interested. One was mentioned here to-day- rural credits. Then there is the Crowsnest pass agreement, and the building of the Hudson Bay railway; the proposals regarding soldier settlement and advances to settlers on crown lands; the question that our group are particularly interested in, old age pensions; the question of the amendment of the Immigration Act, and the amendment to the Criminal Code, both of which passed this House but have been rejected by the Senate. These involve policies that are of great interest to us, and we have a right to know at this stage what is the attitude of the party that advises the Governor General on these matters.
There is just one other consideration that I should like to advance, Mr. Speaker. We have been here for almost six months, and we have as yet accomplished practically nothing. I think hon. gentlemen opposite ought to have applauded that, because I am sure they agree. Perhaps however they do not, because the practical thing accomplished is that we have substituted one party for the other. Perhaps that is what they have been aiming at. But the fact is that for six long months we have done comparatively little but play for position, and apparently the strategists on that side have been better than the strategists on the ex-government side, and so we have the situation we find here to-day. I did not come here to represent the Liberal party or the Conservative party. I was opposed by both, as a matter of fact, in my election. But I came here to try to get certain business of the country done; and now at the end of six months I do not think we have any right, simply because one group has been substituted for the other, to say that because the warm weather is here, and we are all tired, and this proceeding is getting on our nerves, we will pack our trunks and go home to-morrow. Personally I have every desire to facilitate the business of the country; but there are certain policies involved in the estimates which I cannot agree should be passed over without discussion. It is suggested that we could do all this business in a day but I cannot agree-and I think I can speak also for my colleagues in saying this-I cannot agree

to allow millions of dollars of the money of the people to be voted in that fashion. The fact that these estimates have been drawn up or proposed by one party, and that the responsibility for them now devolves on another party, does not obviate my difficulties with regard to the matter. And then there are other questions. To-day I have been calling attention to important public measures that are before this House. More than that, this very day somebody called me into a lobby only a short time ago and asked if there was any chance of dealing with the claims of the Indian tribes of this country.

Hon. gentlemen opposite are pleased to be facetious. I do not wish to 14011-3295
give a silent vote on this important matter. I intend to vote for the amendment but not as expressing absolute adherence to the doctrine that a tariff is undesirable in Canada. In British Columbia we are not unfriendly to some measure of protection; the principal objection to it is the manner in which it is divided. We find that the present conception of protection is that 90 per cent of it shall go to the eastern manufacturers and 10 per cent to those industries of British Columbia which need protection. That is not the form of protection that we idolize in British Columbia. Nevertheless while we are not so strong-we are not strong at all-for the high protection ideas of hon. gentlemen opposite, yet we are not prepared to commit ourselves to the very low tariff ideas of hon. members from the prairies as those ideas have been so often expressed here by hon. gentlemen from those provinces. But he would be a bold man indeed, after the experience of the last few days, who would say he knew what the convictions of some representatives of the prairie provinces really are. In this connection I know that my own political reputation has been entirely ruined. I told my constituents during the election that if there was one thing of which I was sure it was that no matter what would happen, a prairie province representative would not be found voting for the right hon. gentleman who is now the leader of the government because of his well known principles of high protection. My reason for saying that was based on the experience of the past four years during which I have heard-day alfter day, month after month, year after year-hon. members from the prairie provinces, with almost complete unanimity, echo and re-echo the idea that they stood for nothing but a low tariff form of fiscal policy. But how different do we find the situation in the last few days?
Now, there are two reasons why I am voting for this amendment, and I want to state them very briefly. First of all I want to demonstrate to the House and to the country -shall I say rather prove to the country?- whether certain hon. members in placing the present party in power were actuated by the high altruistic principles to which they gave expression and whether, having placed the former opposition in power, they are prepared to revert to their original principles on which they were elected, or whether they will for partisan purposes maintain the present government in power by voting against or abstaining from voting altogether on this amendment, which, after all, is a very simple and very modest echo indeed of the prin-
Supply-Fiscal Policy

ciples which they have so vociferously outlined in this House for the last four years.
My second motive in voting for this amendment is to demonstrate if I can to the right hon. leader of the government, or to his deputy for the moment in the House the absolute need, I think, of an appeal to the country and of a general election before this House meets again. There have been rumours -I suppose I aim in order in mentioning this; they have been mentioned in the press, let alone in the corridors-that in some way the right hon. gentleman who leads the present government is committed to the principle that he must carry on in this House and will be unable to go to the country. I hope that is a mistake; I hope there is no truth in these rumours at all. I am convinced that both sides-the best elements of them at any rate-the most intelligent and thoughtful men in both the great political parties have been convinced for months that the only possible solution of the existing situation is an appeal to the country, and a great deal of what we have witnessed lately has been mere jockeying for position to settle which side would 'have the benefits of holding the reins of power When an election came.
There was no difficulty on the part of the Conservatives in framing an amendment expressing want of confidence in the Liberal government which would be satisfactory to their followers, because a Conservative has no confidence in a Liberal government at any time; but when it came to a question of enlisting the support of other groups in the House it was necessary to present something more than a mere declaration of want of confidence. And so a melange was prepared containing a varied and weird mixture of incoherent political crimes. We had Senator Bureau offered to us if we liked to vote in condemnation of wrongdoing on his part, although he was only mildly censured in the formal report. Then we had the case of the ex-Minister of Customs and Excise suggested for attack if we liked to go in that direction. Then there was the suggestion that a great deal Of liquor was being consumed in the country; and finally there was the suggestion-not so much in the House as in the corridors-that certain dark and mysterious revelations could be and had been made in connection with the Duncan report. Allusion was made in particular to a certain diary which would shock humanity if it were made public. Now, I took the trouble to go downstairs to the office where all reports of such a nature are filed and where I am told the Duncan report was filed, and I find nothing at all to bear out the suggestion or reference 
to this mysterious diary-which I believe, if not actually successful, at least was the means by which an attempt was made to obtain the support of one or two members. As nearly as I can find out, that diary never had any existence, and if it was produced, it was in an utterly unauthorized way and for an ignoble purpose.
I said I wanted to try to convince the leader of the government of the urgent necessity for an election. I would ask him, can he proceed and meet the House next year, relying on what has proved to be such unreliable support in the past? Do we want a continuation of the situation which we have to-day? The recent votes in the House present enough evidence of contradiction without anything else. It may be said, "Well after all, there was no harm in co-operation." Hon. members of the Progressive group told us last night that they had co-operated with the late government. That was perfectly correct and proper, and I have nothing to find fault with in that remark. I myself indulged in a form of co-operation with the government of the day, and submitted certain legislation and certain administrative policies that I wanted adopted, in return for which I would assist the government through the session. I have no shame in that confession. It was cooperation of a distinct type, and a great portion of our desired legislation I received. I am not going into the conduct of other hon. members; I Will only speak for myself Having made an arrangement of that kind, whether right or wrong, that is my responsibility; but if after having made that arrangement I then voted for the resolution or the form of censure, which contained no greater principle than a desire to turn out the Liberal party, the position I would have put myself in would have been very untenable from the ordinary man's point of view. The reason I took that action is that, member of parliament as I am, and politician as I have been accused of being, I still have some lingering remains of the honour involved in an agreement, even if not expressed in legal terms. I still think that if a man makes an honourable agreement with anybody, and it is carried out honourably by the other party, it does behoove a gentleman to comply with the terms of it as he understands them. If I had not done so, I would have held myself to have broken faith in an honourable agreement, to have betrayed the government, and to have betrayed myself, and taken shelter under the excuse that the hon. ex-Minister .of Customs bad done something which I would have asked him to do under exactly similar cir-

Sup-ply-Fiscal Policy
cumstances. I want to warn the right hon. leader of the government, do not go in for co-operation, have no truck or trade with the sons of Amalek, whose conception of co-operation is, as was so wittily expressed the other day by the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird), to get all the benefits they can and let someone else take the responsibility. I want to warn the government against that course.
It is against my personal interest to have an election before holding another session. Nevertheless I am hoping that this motion will carry, or if defeated, that it will be defeated by such a close vote that it will convince the leader of the government that it is impossible for him to carry on. In either case my object will be obtained, and an election will be brought on. I believe it is the only thing to save the country in the present situation.

I do not intend to give a silent vote upon this important question. At the beginning of this session we agreed to support the government on a programme of legislation, and while they may not have done all we would like them to have done, I was not going to break faith before one session at least was concluded. Last night, through indisposition, I did not remain in the House, and did not give my grounds for the vote I cast. Many votes have been brought on this session with no other object than to divide the little group in this corner, who have had the responsibility of deciding on most important matters, and on questions of policy between the two parties in this House. I must say that there were many influences at work which divided this group as it did last evening. One of these was the Alberta natural resources question. When this new government took office we thought some policy would be enunciated, both on the tariff and on these questions that now stand on the order paper. Not one word has come from the government benches since they have taken office. I must say that I felt very keenly last night and was tempted to vote along with some of my Alberta friends who were much interested in this great question. I feel very keenly regarding any question of privilege regarding class, creeds, nationalities, provincial or vocational, in this whole Dominion. I want to see these two great provinces put on an equal footing with every other province, and I did expect that when this matter was on the order paper our friends who have now taken office would pronounce some policy in regard to it. The fact is that they have been afraid to do so, for some reason or other. What their policy is we do not know.
Then again we have the fact that the leader of the government (Mr. Meighen) says we should uphold the government now to carry out the legislation of the session and that the business of the country should go on. We have been here, Mr. Speaker, six months, and three months of that time has been wasted by those who are now occupying the government benches. During that time the business of the country might have been put through, and by this time most of us would have been enjoying the comfort of our homes.
I have been in this city since January 5;
I have not seen my home since, because it is too far to travel back and forth. Three full months have been wasted by those who are appealing now to this little group to enable them to carry on the business of the country.
This group is the deciding body on all questions at the present time. It is a terrible responsibility to assume, but the fact that there are a number of Progressives sitting in this corner to-day is evidence that a large section of the people in the Dominion are not content with present conditions. Parties are playing politics for political expediency and not for the country's welfare. Year after year this proceeding has gone on, and I am happy to say that, although an election was called last year-said to be called for the purpose of eliminating the third party-the third party will not be eliminated. You may kill the body, but the spirit is still there. The reason for the mess we are in to-day, the reason for the spectacle we are presenting before the country and before the whole world-enough to humiliate any Canadian patriot and make him ashamed of his own country and his countrymen-is that the Conservative party at the beginning of the session were not willing to accept a majority vote. They determined to oust the government by any means whatsoever, and since they could not do so on policy they expected to do it by abuse. It was no common thing to hear members of the Conservative party on this side shouting, "If you don't get out, we will push you out. Why don't you get out? Resign; you cannot function." The fact is that they were bad losers; they could not accept the majority vote, and now we find ourselves still here with the country's business unfinished.
I could not either yesterday or on any previous occasion vote for the party opposite to bring about what has been freely referred to in the last few days as political purity. I was asked in common with others to vote, for the purpose of bringing about political
Supply-Fiscal Policy

purity, for a party who still harbour among their numbers men who crucified their brothers at the front during the war by sending them worthless supplies at profiteering prices. I was asked to vote to bring about political purity through the instrumentality of a party who, during their last administration, were guilty of the most heinous crimes in carrying out their policy of privilege and favouritism, and the granting to certain people of some of the country's hard earnings for which no return was given. Class privilege, favouritism and corruption have existed to an extent that knew no bounds and such as, in my opinion, no country in the world has ever known.
