Mr. Speaker, before six
o'clock I was dealing with the cause of the crisis facing this House at present and the responsibility of the government which is now appealing to the Progressive party to support it so that the business of the country may go on.
Being a representative of the agriculturists of Saskatchewan, I cannot see my way clear to support the present government. I pointed out this afternoon that that party when in power on a former occasion has been guilty of some of the greatest crimes that could be committed against certain classes in this country-crimes which they committed in the carrying out of their policy of favoritism, class privilege and corruption. During the years of the war they allowed profiteering to go on unhindered throughout the manufacturing centres of the Dominion, while the farmers had to suffer confiscation of their products at prices sometimes below the cost of production. At a time when wheat would have fetched a price to give us something for cur trouble, it was commandeered at $2.21 a bushel, and we had to pay the freight to Fort William, which freight was increased by over 30 per cent, for during their term of *office the government stole from the farmers the statutory protection which we then enjoyed under what is known as the Crowsnesfc pass agreement. That agreement was worth about $25,000,000 a year to the people of western Canada. Its suspension was continued from year to year, but in 1921 the government promised to restore the agreement in time for the new crop to be hauled at the rates therein provided. However, by order in council, or some other autocratic means,
fMr. Fvanf.l
the Crowsnest pass rates were not restored at that time and the farmers of the west lost another $25,000,000. I say the government confiscated our products at that time at prices which did not allow the cost of production to be reaped by the farmer, while profiteering in all lines of manufactured goods took place, even in munitions and other supplies for the front as well as in foodstuffs and other commodities that were needed in this country. At the same time a per cent higher duty was placed on all our supplies.
When dealing with these great questions of political purity and political policy, Mr. Speaker, I ask this House to-day: Does the customs investigation reveal anything to equal the Home Bank scandal of those days, when for seven years, from 1916 onwards, the very Finance department itself was prostituted to keep going a defunct institution that should have been closed out? It has now cost this country some millions of dollars to reimburse, only partially, those depositors who lost their all in that institution. Broken homes and broken lives, and even suicides, are to be found to-day along the trail from the door of the Finance department to the door of the defunct Home Bank. Again, during the years that the Conservatives were in power they inaugurated a most systematic and tyrannical application of the dumping clause, which practically closed out some of our best cooperative companies in western Canada, making it impossible for them to distribute goods on a co-operative basis.
Taking all these things into account, Sir, I cannot support the present government. The whole debacle of corruption in the Customs department to-day is due to the policy of the Tory party. Favoritism and privilege have been the means of farming the workers during the last forty years in this country; large concerns have been allowed to settle their profiteering balances by promissory notes, while farmers in western Canada have been sent to prison for not making income tax returns when the poor beggars had nothing on which to pay income tax. Promissory notes of these big corporations have been taken in settlement of taxes, some for a3 much as $800,000. Talk about loss of revenue! Who is responsible for that; to what is the present debacle due? It is due to the maintenance of the rankest kind of feudalistic bondage the world has ever seen. You have a combination of evils here; trade restrictions for one thing, robbing the public of their earnings and of their right to buy and sell. When you couple this with the debasing liquor traffic it makes a combination of evils

Supply-Fiscal Policy
with which no nation can cope. We place a number of men in the position of administering an evil law and expect them to be clean; can it be done? I am afraid our professional politicians on both sides of the House have been guilty of receiving doles from these distillers for election campaign funds, so how can we expect clean politics where this sort of thing takes place?
The smuggling evil to-day is simply a backwash of the flow which we have allowed to go freely into a friendly country, without much effort at prevention. That, together with the effort to prevent workers from exercising their rights, is the cause of all our trouble to-day, and speeches in this House during the past six months have shown that it is the intention of the Conservative party to carry on the same policy, which I cannot support. When I look at the mad race for power made by that party, and the sort of thing that has been appearing on the Conservative press throughout the country I find a spectacle humiliating to any patriotic Canadian. While our own group may be divided, our very presence here is an evidence that the people of Canada long for something better. I have said before, and I will say again, that I do not believe this thing can be cleaned up by those who have been connected with the bondage of the past, and I have no hesitation in supporting this amendment.

Before the House goes actually into committee of supply, the Finance minister will bring down the estimates by message from the Governor General, and when the message has been read in English and French by Mr. Speaker, or by the clerk at the table, the minister will move "that the said message, together with the estimates accompanying the same, be referred to the committee of supply. "The order of the day for the House to go into committee of supply having been read, the Speaker will put the question-"That I do now leave the chair." The same question is always
Supply-Fiscal Policy

put whenever the House is to go into committee of supply in order to afford an opportunity to members to -propose amendments.
On this point it is observed by an eminent authority that the ancient constitutional doctrine that the redress of grievances is to be considered before the granting of supplies, is now represented by the practice of permitting every description of amendment to be moved on the question for the speaker leaving the chair, before going into committee of supply or ways and means. Upon other orders of the day, such amendments must be relevant, but here they are permitted to relate to every question upon which a member may desire to offer a motion; the same practice is now followed very extensively in the Canadian Commons; but there are certain limitations to this right. Only one amendment can be moved to the question, "that Mr. Speaker do now ieave the Chair. If that amendment is negatived, a discussion on other questions may be raised but no other motion can be proposed.
On this authority I submit that any question may be debated.

Having listened to the arguments on both sides, I should think that it would be an easy matter, even though the question is rather technical, for hon. members to conform themselves to the practice as indicated in Bourinot. As Bourinot observes, only one amendment is permissible to the motion that the Speaker leave the Chair for the House to resolve itself into committee of supply. In the event of such amendment being negatived, Bourinot, at page 420, says that a discussion on other questions may be raised but that no other motion shall be proposed. At page 421 he says further:
When an amendment has been moved to the Question for the Speaker to leave the Chair, discussion should be properly confined to its subject matter. When an amendment is negatived, a debate may be raised when the Speaker again puts the question, on the general policy of the government, or on some other subjeot, not embraced within the exceptions just mentioned.
I have not by me the amendment which was voted down a moment ago, but as I 
recollect it has reference to past declarations on the part of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) who formerly led the opposition, from which declarations it is argued that it would be dangerous, in the interest of the country, to support the right hon. gentleman's fiscal policy. The amendment embodying that contention having been rejected, I take it that this retrospective feature of the tariff declarations of the present Prime Minister may not be 'further debated That is clearly inferred from Bourinot. i quote again the precedent cited by Bourinot at page 421:
This question arose in the session of 1876. An amendment having been negatived, it was urged by a member that no further debate could take place on the original question; but Mr. Speaker Anglin observed- "The House has not yet resolved that I leave the chair, and that question is consequently still before the House; and gentlemen who have not yet spoken are in order, and are permitted to speak on almost every question.''
That is to say, they could speak "on almost every question " except the one just then disposed of by the House. I rule therefore that hon. members must confine themselves to other issues and refrain from any further discussion of the particular question upon which the House has just voted. May I observe at this juncture that it would facilitate matters and would make for greater celerity if hon. members on both sides would abstain from unnecessary interruptions.

I would suggest
that my hon, friend go and take some lessons in entomology. Now if my hon. friends in the Progressive party consider that they are justified in transferring their allegiance from us to the high tariff group, it is no business of ours so long as they can satisfy their constituencies of the soundness of their position.
This question which we have been discussing is apparently associated with the probability or the improbability of a dissolution. There is no reason why the two things should be associated but inasmuch as the Speaker has ruled that we may discuss almost any subject at all apart from the tariff I want to emphasize the fact that no matter how we vote or when we prorogue a dissolution is bound to come. How do I know? Well, I know the feelings of hon. gentlemen who have

Supply-Fiscal Policy
to sit opposite. We ourselves have gone through six months of more or less excruciating agony, wondering at every moment what was going to happen next, and the only gratifying feature of that trial has been the knowledge that during that time, with the aid of our associates, we have been able to put a good deal of first class legislation on the statutes of Canada. We have made reductions in taxation, we have restored the penny postage, and we have done other things for which the country will be grateful. That, as I say, is the gratifying feature of the situation so far as we are concerned; and because of what we suffered, because of my own experience, I feel a certain amount of sympathy for hon. gentlemen opposite now that they are starting to sweat, so to speak. Just as we could not stand indefinitely the humiliation of being over there, neither can they. By the time they prorogue and get out of this House they will know what it is to occupy those benches. No doubt they are wishing that that time were here already. But so long as they are here they will be subject to criticism not half as bad as they levelled at us, and I feel they will allow themselves to be' forced into a dissolution just as soon as prorogation takes place.
Is there any hon. gentleman in this House who is so simple as to think that by voting for the government he is going to escape a dissolution? Well, I have a lot of sympathy for him. It would seem to indicate that certain promises have been held out. That would do no harm to those to whom the promises were given, but I would ask my hon. friends opposite, how are they going to carry out those promises? Public sentiment is superior to their wishes. The whole country is crying out for a showdown-for a general election. I am not such an extreme party man that I do not think there is a place for Independents in this parliament, but I do think the public affairs of the country cannot continue to be deadlocked as they are at the present time. Already a crisis of tremendous gravity has grown out of this situation from the bringing into existence of this government by means of a most unnatural birth, which was brought about as the result of the deception that the present Prime Minister must have practised on the crown in convincing the crown that he and his party could carry on the national affairs satisfactorily and for a reasonable length of time. There must have been deception, otherwise the crown would not have taken his advice and refused dissolution, thus bringing this government into existence, believing they could carry on better than wo
could. The responsibility for that act does not, as has already been said, devolve on the crown but on its advisers. But in my estimation there will be an election before the snow flies, and I am sure every hon. gentleman who has the cause of good government and the interest of Canada at heart will welcome that day.
It may be that those who voted-unnaturally under ordinary circumstances-with the present government, felt that they had one of two choices: either to help kill themselves or to help kill this government; and, incidentally, to make sure of not having a dissolution by voting against the government* This side of the House has already put itself on record as being in favour of a dissolution. When the former Prime Minister advised His Excellency to dissolve this House, everybody knew our views on the question. We have no formal -declaration from the other side of the House what their views are, and undoubtedly the hope is that by retaining this government in power there will be another session of this parliament. Well, I have too much respect for the historic traditions of my opponents on the other side of the House to think they would stand the humiliation which they would certainly have to submit to if they attempt to carry on for another year. That is why I think we will have an election before the snow flies.
There is another question in the offing, Mr. Speaker, and that is the tremendous constitutional question which has been raised as the result of the birth of this government under such extraordinary and exceptional circumstances. That is a question of paramount gravity, and there is far more involved in it than there is in the question of tariff. Something has happened in this country that has not happened in the British Isles for a hundred years, something that has not happened in Canada since confederation. What is going to be done about it?

I do not think I can be blamed for that desire.
The motion before the House when the amendment was moved was that the House should go into committee of Supply. I think it is the duty of this House to vote supply. In my opinion the amendment was moved, for possibly two purposes:	First, to prevent
the House granting His Majesty supply; and, second, to put some of us who want to expedite the business of the House in an unpleasant position. That is the misfortune of any member who comes to this House to try to transact the business of the country and not to play politics. There is always somebody on one side of the House or the other whose chief concern is to get some of us in bad with the people we are trying to represent and serve. subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: To put in an uncomfortable position any members who wish that the House should go into committee of Supply.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
My hon. friend seems to
be in a particular hurry to go home. Why did he ask suspension of the rules in order that he might move an amendment himself?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Simply so we would not be put in the position that in the last seven business days the House would automatically go into committee of Supply, which would prevent any member moving an amendment to voice any grievance that he might have.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Then why deprive us of
that right?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: I am not depriving any hon. member of that right.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: You surely are.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the business of this House should be concluded. The former government resigned, leaving considerable business unfinished. Certainly those measures which had passed this House, and had been amended by the Senate, should be given a chance to be brought before this House again to be discussed and if thought fit, given third reading. Otherwise the work of this session would be wasted. I am very tired of the party warfare which is carried on in this House. Hon. members to my right will admit, I think, that it was carried on by the members opposite for five months, but since their transfer to the other side of the chamber the party warfare is carried on just the same by those who now form the official opposition. So far as I can see we are between the devil and the deep sea. The ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) said to-night, as I understood him at least, that there was more fun on this side of the House. I think he is right. But, Mr. Speaker, is that what he came here for? I want to know if the members of this House are justified in drawing $4,000 a year just for fun.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
He is not asking to go
home.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: You want your indemnity and then to go home without working at all.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Cannot my hon.
friend appreciate the fact that you can have fun out of your work? Work is drudgery without the fun associated with it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Yes, I can appreciate that all right, but I have heard people outside of this House say, "What is the use of paying 60 cents to get into Keith's theatre when you can see a better vaudeville Aow in the House of Commons?"

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Does my hon.
friend think he makes a contribution?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
This is very funny to some
of my hon. friends. Now may I say that when we came to Ottawa six months ago some gentlemen sitting to my right, who are very fond of interrupting me just now, were very anxious to secure the support of hon. members sitting in this comer of the House.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: If my hon. friend is referring to me I would ask him to give one single instance when I even spoke to him.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
At that time this group wrote both the then Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition asking their attitude in regard to certain questions in which they were very much interested, one of which was the

Supply-Fiscal Policy
tariff. May I now draw to the attention of the House a few words from the letter of the present Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition:
May I add, though, that on the subject of the tariff I could not in a few words better define our historic and present policy than to quote what the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King on September 8, in the county of Peel, in the province of Ontario, declared to be [the policy of the Liberal party, namely-"a tariff which will help to give us what we need in the way of revenue, and, at the same time safeguard industrial development."
This is the declaration we had from the leader of the present so-called government when we had to consider the question of cooperating with either of the old parties.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Does my hon.
friend understand from that letter that the leader of the present government accepted the tariff policy of the Liberal government, and is that why he and his party voted against the amendment?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
No. I would say that the
tariff policy of either party did not influence my vote to-night one iota.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
It would be very interesting
to know what did influence my hon. friend in his vote.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: I told my hon. friend a few moments ago; if he had not been asleep he might have 'heard me. I voted against that amendment because I think we should attend to the business of the House and get supply voted.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: That is childish.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
I suppose it is childish, but
among all the politicians in this House I consider myself a child. I do not want to take up the time of the House; we should get to business, although I doubt very much if we will. I should like to say, however, that we seem to be fast approaching the time when the Governor General should seriously consider calling on certain members of this House to form a coalition government.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Under rule 19 the hon.
gentleman should not bring into a debate the name of His Excellency. I know he has no sinister motive, but it is not proper to refer to the Governor General in a political discussion.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
I am very sorry to have
transgressed the rules of the House. I feel that possibly what we need, and need soon, is a coalition government in which all groups -a co-operative government, I do not care what you call it-may be represented.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Is that the answer to my
question? It sounds like it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Then possibly party warfare
may cease long enough to allow the business of the session to be concluded. Now I have a word to say to the low tariff men in this House, of whom I hope some are still my friends in spite of my recent vote. My views on the tariff have not changed at all; regardless of how many votes I may give against amendments on motions to go into supply, I do not think my tariff views will change very much. I would still be co-operating with the party which claims to be the low tariff party, and which does contain a number of low tariff men, had it not been for an unfortunate occurrence in one department of that government. I am sorry that in this country we have a system of government under which, if serious trouble occurs in one department, the result seems to be that the whole government must be upset. I wish some members of the late government were still in office, but there is no use in going back and rewashing old linen. I do regret the fact, however, that governments are put out of office in this country because of the misdemeanors of one or two of their members.
There are many other things I would like to say along this line, but I will not be responsible for longer delaying the business of the House; if that business is further delayed the responsibility must be on someone else. As I said last night, physically I am almost at the end of my endurance; if this party warfare is carried on much longer I may be compelled to go home and leave those party warriors to fight it out.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
On the first vote taken yesterday,
after this government assumed the treasury benches, on an appeal from your ruling, Mr. Speaker, the government were defeated by a majority of one. On a subsequent vote they received a majority of twelve; later they had a majority of ten and to-night that majority has been reduced to seven. The hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat, speaking I presume for the group in that corner of the House who saved the government-because you must keep in mind, Sir, the fact that had that group not voted with the government to-night they would have been defeated-said that the only solution now apparent is a coalition government. I submit that that cannot be posted up to-morrow as a verdict in favour of the government; we have it from the hon. gentleman who speaks for that group that he has so little confidence in this government that he suggests a coalition.
520S
Supply-Fiscal Policy

As the hon. gentleman has said, we have worked hard during a long session, I think one of the longest sessions I have attended during the eighteen years I have been in parliament. The independent press of the country, as well as the Tory press, have been telling the country from early in this session that the only solution for Canada to-day is a general election, so that the people may determine what is best. Now having in mind that the government of which I had the honour to be a member had a larger majority in this House than this government has ever registered, having in mind also the difficulties that we had in carrying on, knowing the conditions, and knowing what the Acting Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) will be up against, I submit that they can neither satisfy their friends who financed the advertising which hon. gentlemen opposite profited by during the last election, nor can they satisfy the group to my left under existing conditions, and I submit that the sooner the hon. gentleman to whom His Excellency now looks for advice advises him that he is not able to carry on without certain negotiations, the better. I make this statement so that hon. members may know whether it is true or not, and if not true, may Tefute it:	I
have been told only recently in the lobby that there is a bargain that there shall be two more sessions. Well, I want to know what is going to be the policy of the government during those two sessions, and I think the people of Canada are entitled to know what is going to be their policy. I believe that the gentlemen who financed the advertising which hon. gentlemen opposite enjoyed last fall are also entitled to know that, and what is more, the electors who sent to this parliament the hon. gentlemen who saved this government from defeat to-night are entitled to know it. I am not much interested in what hon. gentlemen down to my left may think, but I am interested in knowing what their electors will think to-morrow morning, and I am interested in knowing what those who throughout this session have been advocating a higher and a higher tariff and their friends who have been urging upon them a higher and a higher tariff will think, and also what the general public of Canada will think. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the only possible solution of this difficulty is not a coalition, but a return to the people, and let the people decide.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what are the terms of this cooperation? That question has been asked by several hon. gentlemen to my right. It is
(Mr. Robb.]
true that from the beginning of this session almost up to to-day, certainly up until the end of last week, a most full and honourable and open system of co-operation has existed between the late government and hon. gentlemen in this party, and it has been admitted on both sides that both groups have lived up to the terms of that co-operation. I am here to say that that is the case. There was perhaps a falling off on the question of the natural resources of Alberta, due to complications affecting the provincial government in Alberta, which possibly provided hon. gentlemen to my right with some meagre excuse for the position in which they found themselves. Let me say, though, that when the late government sat over there and ran away from *its own duty and its own responsibility, it ceased from that moment to have any further claim upon the co-operation of hon. gentlemen in this group. I regret deeply to say that, and I hope that in the future cooperation can again be restored, not only with that group, but with any group that will co-operate with us. We are always willing and open to co-operate, but the day last week on which the Prime Minister of this country decided to fly away from his responsibilities, to fly from possible defeat, to fly from the carrying through of his legislation and his estimates, from that moment on we were placed in an entirely different relation towards him and his ministry.
I am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that the parliamentary institutions of this country, as practised at the present time, are utterly impossible in view of the situation in this House, and there must be a modification of that situation. I think there has been a recognition of that by several hon. members who have thought deeply upon this subject, and it was so stated in no uncertain terms at the outset of this session by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird), and other hon. members in this group, who have constantly indicated to the House their complete dissatisfaction and lack of confidence in the present parliamentary institutions. There has got to be a change of alignment, a change of the method of appointing governments, and of accepting votes upon certain questions.
Let me say definitely at this stage that I for one do not intend to be tricked into voting for any merely political motion. The hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) said that we were here to discuss political questions. We are not here to discuss political questions. We are here to carry on the business of Canada. Let the hon. gentle-

Supply-Fiscal Policy
man take his political discussions to the hustings; there perhaps they may receive a hearing and may have some influence, but political questions such as this motion raises at this stage certainly have no reasonable bearing upon the vote of any hon. gentleman.
Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that to my personal knowledge there is absolutely no cooperation, nor co-operative understanding, nor negotiation, nor arrangment, nor anything of that kind whatever, between the hon. members of this group and the hon. gentlemen who now sit on the government benches. [ personally have not entered into any negotiations with them with respect to this vote, or with respect to my vote on any other question. I go further, and I say that before this group-I speak advisedly, and hon. gentlemen around me can contradict me if I am wrong-can afford to enter into any cooperative arrangement with hon. gentlemen opposite, we shall know what their policy is; we must know it, just as we asked hon. gentlemen now to our right what their policy was. The day we enter into any co-operative arrangement with hon. gentlemen who now sit on the government benches, on that day hon. gentlemen to my right and the public will know it. That arrangement will be just as open and above-board and honourable as the arrangement we had with hon. gentlemen to my right. That day may never come but I tell hon. gentlemen frankly that when it does come they will know it, and there will be no backstairs intrigue to my knowledge and with my consent.
On the particular amendment which has just been voted on, the fiscal policy of this country was absolutely not at stake. If you wish to discuss the fiscal policy of this country -I know I am verging here upon the point of being out of order-I would remind hon. gentlemen to my right that the party to my right, which.now preaches low tariffs, and did under the pressure of the group in this corner of the House and of that able and eloquent little group from Saskatchewan, grant certain reductions in the tariff this year, just as was done last year on agricultural implements, yet in one session in the last four years it brought in a budget announcing the death knell of protection, and the very next year established a policy of tariff stability. In the face of that, what can we think? Can we be expected to get anywhere on such a vague, academic, theoretical question as has been put to us tonight? We do not know, we cannot know, what we are voting on. But as soon as we vote on an 14011-330
issue, we shall record our votes intelligently, and I hope consistently.
One word more, and I am through. I am satisfied that this motion was introduced today, as other motions may be introduced subsequently, for one purpose and one purpose only. The Liberal party is now so anxious to gain control of the election machinery in view of what they hope will be an appeal to the country that they are willing to go to any extreme to get that control. I speak as one from the province of Alberta and for myself I have nothing to fear from an election. I have never personally spent one cent on an election campaign, and I will not. My people have subscribed for my election campaign and they have elected me, and I owed allegiance to no party, to no corporation; no one has any strings on me but my U.F.A.
The United Farmers of Alberta has just completed one of the most successful campaigns that has ever been carried on in that province. We have been swept back again into office, and I have nothing to fear, nor have hon. gentlemen from the province of Alberta sitting around me anything to fear from an election; so I am in a position to be able to say, when charges of an evil and objectionable character are being levelled against me, that the country does not want an election to-day. No one knows that better than hon. gentlemen to my right, and hon. gentlemen who are in touch with business circles in eastern Canada. Those in high authority who have the power to pass the control from one party to another know that just as well as hon. gentlemen in this House know it. That being the case, I say that we would be ill advised indeed to fall into any trap that may be set for us by hon. gentlemen to my right just as we would have been ill advised to fall into the trap set by the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Davis), or by any other hon. member who moves a political motion. So far as I personally am concerned, I will weigh every question on its merits, and if I detect in it a single trace of political motive, distinct altogether from the interests of the country, I shall have no hesitation in voting against it.
It might just happen that in spite of the common sense of some of the members in this House-most of us have some sense but some have a political sense that exceeds their business sense-a situation may arise where even then it may not be possible to carry on. In that case there is but one thing possible, as I view the matter, and that is that some form of co-operative government, just as the hon. member for Macleod suggested,

Supply-Fiscal Policy

should be arranged for and carried on so that the election machinery may be taken out of the hands of political parties, and a disgraceful influence upon the votes of the people of this country be removed from partisan hands for all time. And in entering into a co-operative arrangement of that kind, let Colonel Biggar, the Chief Electoral Officer at the present time, or whoever may be the chief electoral officer at the moment, conduct the federal election. In each constituency each little group or each little party will have its own organization, but as far as the present national control of political machinery is concerned, it is wrong in principle. It is absolutely unsound that political parties- either Liberals, Conservatives or Progressives -should have anything whatever to say about-it.
I have now, I hope, given to my hon. friend the member for Pontiac, and to other hon. gentlemen, my answer to their questions. And may I say in conclusion that it ill becomes these hon. gentlemen who know us, who have known us for four years, and who have co-operated with us, to suggest or to attempt to suggest, as they have done tonight, that we have in any way done anything dishonourable. I will tell my hon. friend everything when there is anything to disclose.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit a question? He has made a statement which I take it is correct. I know him and I believe he is absolutely honest in his statement. But he also said that, as I understood it, we should hurry through this session, prorogue, go home, and then come back here next session in the same state of confusion that now exists without any understanding. If we are to come back, if this parliament is to meet again, we should have some understanding. This country should not be left in the state of chaos it is in to-day without some such understanding. How does my hon. friend think the country is going to accept the position in which it is left to-night if there is no understanding that there is to be another session? If there is an understanding, the nature of it certainly should be explained, although I believe there is no understanding so far as my hon. friend himself is concerned.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
I am not
in a position to solve the horrible problem which is worrying me just as much as it is my hon. friend. I have simply stated the position as it is at this moment. I presume that if it is the desire of my hon. friends to carry on they can do so; but the suggestions

I have made appeal at least to myself, and I hope to every honourable person, as reasonable suggestions for dealing with the situation.
Mr. JEAN J. DENIS (Joliette):	I only
want to say a few words in answer to my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) and my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland). These two gentlemen know that I hold them in high esteem, as I also hold in high esteem all members of the Progressive party and all members . of this House. However, it seems to me that in their utterances to-night there is sudh variance and such a lack of logic that I could not let them pass unchallenged. I see the hon. member for Macleod walking out of the House. He is quite free to do so, but I have told him that I was going to reply to some of his statements and he would do me a great favour by remaining. The hon. member says, "I have earned my indemnity already." With all due deference to the hon. member, foi whom I have every consideration, I ask him: Is that a principle? Hon., members of the Progressive party, and I have no fault to find with them on that score, have come here and contended that they are men of principle; that the two old parties changed their principles but that they themselves adhere to principle. Is it a matter of principle for an hon. member to say, "Once I have earned my indemnity I can go home"?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit me to say that I am quite ready to stay here another month or two months if there is business to be done, but I do not like to remain at this stage of the -proceedings and listen to party warfare. That is the point I thought I was making when I spoke.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
My hon. friend,
perhaps, has not had very much experience in politics. Does he know that since confederation and prior to that time there has never been anything else in the Canadian parliament but party warfare? Does he know that in England at the present time there is party warfare in politics, and that the same condition prevails in every civilized country where there is a parliament?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Is the hon. gentleman not
aware that a great many of us in this comer of the House came down here to try to get away from party warfare, and that we do not want to see politics introduced into the carrying on of the business of the country?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
My hon. friend is
cherishing an illusion. As long as there is a parliament in Canada there will be party warfare-that is, if such an expression is ap-

Supply-Fiscal Policy
propriate, and I do not think it is proper. I know what my hon. friend means. What he objects to is one party fighting against another. My hon. friend will live many years and die an old man I hqpe, but when he reaches an advanced age he will still find the same conditions as to party warfare existing in this parliament that he sees now.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
The hon.
gentleman is too pessimistic.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Long before my
hon. friend was born there was party warfare in this Dominion. Let them read the debates before and since confederation and they will see there has been nothing else but party warfare. Of course when a government has a majority of thirty, forty or fifty, there is ijot very much party warfare; but each time the political parties are divided as they are at the present moment, when there is but a small majority on one side or the other, you will have political warfare; that is inevitable. But do not let us call it party warfare; let us consider it the efforts of two parties working in different directions, both of them having at heart the good of the country and both doing their best to accomplish that desired result. I want to attribute proper motives to the members of every party; but if you insist upon calling the struggles between the parties party warfare you will see bitter fights in this House under present conditions, as well as under altogether different conditions.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Will the hon. member tell us what the bitter fights are all about?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
I want to discuss this matter with my hon. friend in a polite and friendly manner, and for that reason I will not answer his last question but I will tell him this: If he wants to be logical and wants to act in accordance with principle He cannot claim that he wants to go home, because by voting with hon. gentlemen on this side he will bring about that result sooner than he would if he voted with hon. gentlemen opposite. My hon. friend said the amendment this afternoon was purely a political amendment. Let us be frank when we are discussing this matter. Every time a resolution is brought in for political purposes, according to his notion, is he at liberty to vote diametrically opposite to his principles? It is impossible to accept that.
My hon. friends have spoken of co-operation. It is true there has been co-operation between the Liberal and Progressive parties, and had the Liberals of the province of Quebec not been willing to co-operate with the Progressive party, co-operation would have 14011-330J
been impossible. We did co-operate with them, and I am not sorry for it. If we had it to do all over again I would co-operate. But both sides must co-operate. We Liberals from the province of Quebec could live very well without co-operation, and if we did cooperate it was for the reason that I stated at the opening of parliament, that throughout the length and breadth of Canada our party should co-operate with all independent groups and work together for the welfaj-e of our country. That was our object, and in order to attain it I am not ashamed to state to-night that I have voted for more than one measure which in my estimation might have been doubtful if I had considered my province only. But that was not my object. I considered the whole of Canada; I realized that two or three thousand miles from here there were provinces with which we should co-operate, and for that reason I supported those measures. My friends having obtained what they were after, apparently they say, "Now that we have crossed the river, we take our hats and are going home."

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: The only reason I have voted as I have is that one department of the government had got into such a state-and I ielt that some members of the government knew it-that I could not support the then government. I was sorry that the co-operation could not be further carried out.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
I want to be very modest in my words and speech, but I will go further; do my hon. friends of the Progressive party think-their principles being known and recorded; in this House-that co-operation would be easier with the present government than with the group on this side of the House? If there is one hon. member who is of that opinion, I should like to know his name. They cannot contend that, because it would be illogical. I do not want to blame them for their action; they are perfectly free and they have my consideration, esteem and respect, but notwithstanding all that I cannot bring myself to the belief that co-operation is easier with the Tory party than with the Liberal party. Co-operation with the Tory party is impossible; and that has been demonstrated during the present session. Just think of the logic of these estimable gentlemen. They want co-operation, but in the meantime, while they are claiming co-operation, they are supporting a party with which they cannot co-operate.
My hon. friend said they would like to have coalition. I do not know if it is new to my hon. friend, but it is not new to others. I am going to tell my hon. friends something to take with them to Saskatchewan and Al-
Supply-Secretary of State

berta. Referring to coalition, do my hon. friends from the Progressive party know, or do they ignore the fact, fhat for two or three years at least, and perhaps more, very prominent people belonging to both parties in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario have claimed that those two provinces should go hand in hand and co-operate in order to govern this country? If my hon. friends do not know that, they do not know very much, because it is no secret. I am not divulging any secret, and moreover I was not a party to it. I am simply repeating what I have heard time and time again, and no one can go to Toronto or Montreal without meeting among the business men of those two largest cities in this Dominion many who will tell my Conservative friends on the one hand and the Liberals on the other that they should co-operate, and that there must not be any feud between Quebec and Ontario. If there is any misunderstanding between those provinces, remember that our interests are identical and that they should join hands and work together. Do my hon. friends know that Quebec has 65 members and Ontario 82? My hon. friends should make the addition and find out what it represents. They ask for cooperation and coalition. If we ever have coalition between Ontario and Quebec, the Progressives might not see their policy advanced very much. I do not want to threaten anybody, but, in common with my hon. friends from Macleod (Mr. Coote) and Bow River (Mr. Garland) I want the business of the country carried on and am willing to let politics go in order to gain that end. I hope my hon. friend will not think for one moment that I was speaking of him in a personal way. Although I do not know him very well personally, he knows I have a great deal of esteem for him. To-night I am speaking with a purpose. I want him to consider my statement, not because it comes from me, but because I am voicing the opinion of many who think as I do. I advise the hon. gentleman to read Hansard before he goes home and consider once more what I have just said concerning Quebec and more particularly Ontario.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee of Supply, Mr. Duff in the chair.

speechtext: It is all very well for the leader of the government to rise in his place and with a gesture to the gallery say, "Gentlemen, you will certainly piass these estimates, because they are yours." So far as the main estimates are concerned, there is no doubt we take full responsibility for their preparation, and we hope the country will give us credit for the estimates as they are presented to the House. I ask my hon. friend now and the other hon. members of the newly formed government sitting around him, whether or not they will undertake to spend the money that we are voting to them to-night? That is a question to which the people of Canada are entitled to have an affirmative or negative reply. Therefore I think before we proceed further in rushing these estimates through at the rate of millions of dollars per hour we should have some assurance that the government is going to use every reasonable effort to expend the money voted according to the wishes of this House. Without that assurance I do not think we should continue at this headlong pace passing estimates which may never be expended.

I am not criticising the officers; I think they did their duty in preparing the estimates, but I would like to know whether the opinions of these responsible officers will be carried out or whether my hon. friends are merely voting these estimates in order to close parliament at the earliest possible opportunity and get back to their homes, leaving perhaps for another year the real expenditure of money required for the public service, in order that they may get the benefit of having placed the amounts in the estimates and in order that they may tell the people of Canada. speechtext: Privy councillors are not permitted to walk into the council chamber, sit around the table, and pass whatever orders they may like, to give each other official positions. If that were the case there is no reason why my erstwhile colleagues and myself should not have walked into the council chamber and sat down at the table with whoever was prepared to assume the position of Prime Minister of this country and assign positions to ourselves that would enable us to control the expenditure of public moneys to the extent necessary to carry on the administration of public affairs for a year.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Would it not all depend on whether my right hon. friend and those who sit about him were invited to do so by a .privy councillor who had been Called upon by His Excellency the Governor General to form an administration?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
No, I am afraid it does not. I think my hon. friend will find that there are two oaths which everyone takes who is called upon to perform the duties of a minister of the crown. One oath taken
is that- of Privy Councillor, which a number of us in this chamber this evening have taken.' But the fact that we are members of His Majesty's Privy Council gives us no right whatever to be ministers of the crown or to be acting as ministers of the crown. There are gentlemen in the other House who have taken the oath as privy councillors and are privy councillors, but they have no right by virtue of that oath to be ministers or acting ministers. It was never contemplated that the government of the country should be carried on by gentlemen who had not taken the oath of office with respect to the administration of the departments with which they were concerned. It was never contemplated that one single individual could take an oath as Prime Minister and president of the Privy Council, and any other portfolio he wished, and by virtue of that one solitary oath be able to place in office immediately a number of his fellow members of the House of Commons, members of his own political party, and thus carry on the government of the country.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Has not tl\e Prime Minister from time immemorial been entitled to call upon other members of the Privy Council to administer temporarily the affairs of a particular department without such member taking an oath with respect to that department?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FISCAL POLICY ENUNCIATED BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: After a government has been formed and ministers of the crown have taken the oath to administer the departments to Which they are assigned, certainly an acting minister may be appointed to act in the place of a minister already entrusted with a portfolio and properly sworn in. But what I want to make clear to the House and to the country this evening is that of this entire cabinet there is not a single member who has taken any oath to administer a single department of the government; and yet these gentlemen come before us with estimates and ask us to vote hundreds of millions of dollars. We have voted some thousands of dollars already just to see how calmly they would take the process, and how rapidly they are prepared to vote millions of dollars to themselves without having any authority whatever to a^k this House for a single dollar. I say there is not a single minister of this .administration sitting in his seat to-night who is entitled to ask this House to vote him a single dollar.

I hope he will not think I am speaking disrespectfully, because I respect his years and his great ability, but since he makes the kind of charge which I understand he does make against me at the moment, I think he will have to listen to what I have to say about constitutional practice in changing ministries. The practice with respect to resignation, as I understand it-and perhaps my hon. friend will tell me if I am wrong-is that if the Prime Minister is of the opinion there should be a dissolution of parliament his duty is so to advise His Excellency the Governor General, just as he advises His Excellency the Governor General in regard to other matters [DOT]of concern to the state. He might assume that something less than a dissolution would be sufficient to meet the needs of the state, in which event he would advise His Excellency in accord with his belief. May I say, in considering what I was called upon as prime minister to consider, that after noting the
proceedings in this House last week I came to the conclusion that this House could not with dignity and honour to itself continue to carry on the public business of the country. I came to the conclusion that to attempt to carry on public business with a condition such as we were witnessing towards the end of last week would be to bring the great and honourable institution of parliament more or less into disrepute; and having that view I was obliged to consider whether it was desirable to attempt any longer to carry on parliament. I went to His Excellency and said I would not longer take the responsibility of carrying on as prime minister, believing that the best interests of the state were not being served by any government attempting to carry on under the circumstances which now exist, and I advised His Excellency as to the next step to be taken which in the circumstances seemed to me should be dissolution.
Under different circumstances I might have advised His Excellency to send for some other hon. member of this House to form an administration, had I believed any other hon. member of this House could form an administration and be able to carry on better than I was able to do. But I did not honestly believe that. The only person I could think of whom it would be at all fitting and proper for me to ask His Excellency to call on, if His Excellency was to be asked to call on any hon. member, was the right hon. leader of the opposition of the day. Well the right hon. leader of the opposition of the day had had no support from this House of Commons from the moment it came into being up to the moment I sought to advise His Excellency, and the main question that was discussed all through the session, the main issue in the election, the issue that decided whether hon. members were to be returned to this House, and as to which side they were to sit on when they were returned, vas according to the present Prime Minister the great fiscal issue on which on an amendment to go into supply, we had a discussion this afternoon. In those circumstances how, when the majority of hon. members in this House differed from the Prime Minister on fiscal policies, the most important of all policies, could I possibly advise His Excellency that the right hon. gentleman was capable of forming a ministry and carrying on? It was impossible, just as my hon. friend says, honestly to advise His Excellency that I believed any other member of this House should carry on the government of the country, and I had to consider that. I am frank to say-well it is not for me to relate

A prime minister may 'have a feeling that there are certain policies he is not in a position to carry through which possibly other groups in the House are in a position to put through, and that in the public interest should be carried through. In cases of that kind a prime minister might go to the crown or its representative and say, I am not in a position to carry this policy through; I cannot carry on the business of this country myself, but I believe that so and so, whoever he may be, would be able to carry on, and I would ask Your Excellency, or Your Majesty -as the case might be-to call on him. In that event His Excellency would take the course, I presume, of calling on whoever was named. May I say this, that I believe it has been represented to His Excellency by the present Prime Minister that he is able to carry on the business of this House in a manner which is dignified and proper. He could not possibly be Prime Minister to-day on any other score; he must have told His Excellency that, or His Excellency would never have asked him to be Prime Minister. But having said that to the crown representative he owes it to the honour of the crown to implement his words, and I say it is not to the honour of the crown that he should seek to put into the seats of the ministry a group of gentlemen not one of whom has taken any oath of office, and call that the responsible ministry which is to advise His Excellency the Governor General with respect to all the affairs of this country. I say I cannot think of any act more irresponsible or unconstitutional than that. When the present Prime Minister went to His Excellency and said, as he must have said, "I am prepared to take the responsibility of Your Excellency having refused dissolution to Mr. King", he had to pledge himself to His Excellency by his word that he was able to carry on where I was unable to carry on. Now let me repeat that. If I had believed that the present Prime Minister could do anything of the kind I would have so advised His Excellency, and would have been very glad to have had His Excellency send for my right hon. friend and give him a chance.

The parallel
that my hon. friend suggests was not at the beginning of the MacDonald administration, but at the close. Mr. Ramsay MacDonald went to His Majesty the King and asked for a dissolution after he had been in office only part of one session, and he got a dissolution. My position, and I take it in the interest of this country, as a self-governing Dominion, is that the Prime Minister of Canada advising His Excellency the Governor General is in precisely the same position as the Prime Minister of England advising His Majesty the King. May I say to my hon. friend who has just spoken that any other theory of government reduces this Dominion of Canada from the status of a selfgoverning Dominion to the status of a crown colony. What has been the evolution of our political institutions?
Are we going to have a lot more?

Yes, you are
going to have a lot more. Hon. gentlemen opposite need a good deal of education in the matter of political freedom. I want to make clear the principles for which I have been standing. What is the position of a crown colony? Governors go out from Britain with instructions from the Colonial Office, and they exercise authority which is more or less discretionary with themselves. They call upon individuals to become members of .their councils; they have the appointing to office, and the dismissing from office in certain cases. That was the condition we were in in parts of Canada about a century ago. But since that time there has been a political evolution of considerable proportions in all parts of the British Empire, and what to-day are known as the self-governing Dominions are to my mind, in precisely the same position in the management of their own domestic affairs as is the government of Great Britain with respect to its domestic affairs.
We all know .that.

No, you don't know it, or you would not be sitting where you are. The difference between a crown colony and a self-governing Dominion is that the Governor General of a self-governing Dominion acts upon the advice of his responsible ministers. May I say this, Mr. Chairman:	For one hundred years in Great
Britain there is not .a single instance of a Prime Minister having asked for a dissolution and having been refused it. May I add this further, that since this Dominion was formed, since confederation in 1867, there is not a
[Mr. E. J. Garland.)
single instance where a Prime Minister has advised a dissolution and has been refused it. Is there then no constitutional issue at stake?

We have never had a
usurper before.

You have certainly got one now in the seat of the Prime Minister, and one who is more or less of an expert as a usurper. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the issue that we are face to face with at the present time is one which affects all parts of the British Empire, and it is amongst other reasons because of my belief in and my love for the British Empire that I take the stand that I do in this matter. It is only by a recognition of the fact that the British Empire rests upon the corner stone of responsible self-government in each of the Dominions and in the Mother Country that this great empire can endure; and that is why I feel we are called upon at this time to see that the principle of responsible self-government is fully carried out. I say, Mr. Chairman, that at this time we have at heart the interests not only of Canada, but of South Africa, of Australia, of New Zealand, of Newfoundland, of the Irish Free State, of India, yes, and of the British Isles themselves.
The United States too.

No, not the United States. That shows again how ignorant my hon. friend is. The United States have an entirely different form of government, and a little study of comparative institutions would not do my hon. friend opposite any harm. Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to take up very much more time-
Go on.

Yes, I will go on. I want to make this position clear, so that there can be no mistake as to my attitude in relation to His Excellency the Governor General and the advice which I have tendered. I ask hon. members to listen very carefully to what I am now saying.
I believe that His Excellency the Governor General sincerely believed that the present Prime Minister would be able to carry on the government of this country in a manner befitting and in accordance with British traditions, in a manner which would accord with the recognized principles of responsible government; and believing that, His Excellency undoubtedly asked the present Prime Minister whether he was prepared to assume office on those conditions. Now if the right hon. gentleman can demonstrate to the country,

if he has demonstrated to this House and this parliament, that he is able to do that, after what we have seen and are witnessing in this so-called ministry presented to us to-night, then I say that His Excellency's judgment in the matter has been sound and right, and there is no criticism to offer. But I do say this, that if-and this is subject to something further I shall have to say-if by any chance it should appear that we have another day of the character we have had to-day, when the government can only be carried on by ministers not one of whom has taken an oath of office, then I think it would be time for His Excellency to ask himself the question whether the right hon. gentleman who assumed to carry on this House has carried out his undertaking. If he has not carried it out, then, as I have already said, it is the duty of the present Prime Minister not to wait until His Excellency is obliged to send for him but to return to His Excellency the Governor General and relieve His Excellency of the tremendous responsibility which he is carrying at this hour. I say that it is the duty of the right hon. the Prime Minister at this moment to lose no time in returning to His Excellency the Governor General and telling His Excellency that he has attempted to carry on but that he finds he is confronted with a situation, parliament being in session, which does not allow him to carry on in a manner which will help to maintain respect and regard for parliamentary institutions, and that therefore he asks to be relieved of tendering to His Excellency further advice. It will then be for His Excellency to say what course he will take. Until His Excellency has had that opportunity, and until I see what course His Excellency takes as a consequence of it, I for one do not intend to offer any criticism whatever of the constitutionality of the course taken up to the present time. I do not think I can make ihy position clearer than that.
Now, may I return again to the situation with which we are confronted? I asked hon. gentlemen opposite a moment ago whether any of them had taken the oath of office. Not one has. I asked them how they were appointed? They said they were all appointed by order in council. Now look at the situation: We have a Prime Minister who has taken an oath. I ask hon. members to remember this-the Prime Minister has taken an oath. He has not, given a mere promise or undertaking to do something, but has taken a solemn oath which relates to the crown itself, with all that pertains to the sacredness of parliamentary institutions. That oath obliges him to see that the crown's name 14011-3311
in all particulars is protected; that the crown or its representative shall not by any act of his be brought into public discussion. May I say that is only through the act of the present Prime Minister that any mention has come to be made of His Excellency the Governor General at the present time-only through his act. He has taken his oath to see that the government of this country is carried on in a manner which will not reflect upon the crown and all that the crown stands for in conserving the liberties and freedom of the people under responsible government. Now, I shall give the Prime Minister the opportunity to-night of thinking over the position in which he has placed His Excellency the Governor General, over the position in which he has placed His Majesty's representative in this country, over the position in which he has placed the King himself,-because he is acting as one who is advising the crown through its representative- and I say to him that if he will read my words in the morning, if perchance he cannot hear them now, he should consider very carefully how much longer he is going to keep His Excellency in the position of great suspense which he must be in at the present time with respect to whether or not his act has been constitutional or justified, and for what he does in that regard the present Prime Minister will be judged by the people of this country and by posterity itself.
Now that right hon. gentleman, having taken the oath of office, proceeds to appoint his ministry. May I again recall to hon. gentlemen opposite what I said a moment ago about the manner in which orders in council are passed and what is essential in that regard. Four members of the cabinet are supposed to constitute a quorum. How was the first order in council passed, appointing hon. gentlemen opposite? I suppose the hon. gentleman who is leading the House at the moment was appointed by the first order in council. Therefore I ask my hon. friend who were present at the cabinet meeting when he was appointed? What was the quorum that enabled the Prime Minister to pass an order in council and present it to His Excellency? I say that if the Prime Minister of this country went to His Excellency the Governor General with an order in his hand appointing certain gentlemen opposite ministers of state or acting ministers of state, when there was only himself to sit in council and pass it, and asked His Excellency to sign that order, he committed the most autocratic and unconstitutional act t'. Mr. Chairman, I think it is only due to my right hon. leader that I should review the situation in a very few sentences. By the act of the ex-Prime Minister the position of leader of the government was vacated. His Excellency then called in the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen to form a government. He had to consider whether he would ask the House to adjourn for a few weeks in order to allow him time to form a ministry and meet the House, or whether in view of the dying hours of the session, admitted by all, it would not be advisable to ask the House to allow the legislation on the order paper to pass, together with the estimates, and prorogue parliament. In doing that he stated to the House-in what I think was a courteous message delivered by my hon. friend who is leading the House in his name, a message presented within twenty-four hours after his Excellency had requested the right hon. gentleman to form a ministry- the situation, and closed with these words:
So soon aa prorogation takes effect Mr. Meighen will immediately address himself to the task of constituting a government in the method established by custom.
You cannot do that while the House is in session.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Customs and Excise; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Minister of Trade and Commerce; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The presemt plan is merely to meet an unusual,.if not unprecedented, sitiuation.
Had the House at that time or on two subsequent occasions rejected the Prime Minister's suggestion, it would have made a great difference. Last night there was offered1 a resolution from the opposition benches which wa3 ,a challenge to the government's authority. ,The House sustained the government on that occasion by a majority of 12 and subsequently by a majority of 10. To-day we met the House, and the right hon. gentleman himself, leading the opposition, offered a direct vote of want of confidence in the government. That resolution was debated at length and was finally rejected by a majority of 7.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I submit that my right hon. friend is going beyond his right of criticism when he interprets the opinion of the House. I say the House can only interpret its opinion by its registered vote, and by its registered vote up to this minute the House has sustained the government, admittedly, as

My hon. friend is absolutely right. I am not going to offer what I fl.m about to say in criticism of the ex-Prime Minister. It will be recalled that when he tendered his resignation-most unexpectedly I think to us all so far as the moment was .concerned-the suggestion was made by my right hon. leader that under the extraordinary circumstances a conference would be advisable between the right hon. gentleman now leading the opposition and himself as to the best method of carrying on the business of the House with the least inconvenience to all members concerned. Through a difference of opinion between the right hon. gentleman that offer was not accepted. But I wish to draw to the attention of hon. gentlemen what I think will convince them that our procedure has been quite constitutional in every respect. The present Prime Minister having presented his address to the House, and having been sustained in these two votes, is, I submit, quite entitled to carry on. The right hon. leader of the opposition calls in question the .orders in council appointing the acting ministers. This procedure was carefully considered by the law officers of the crown and by those who advise the ministers in these matters, and every constitutional requirement was observed.
One other thing I desire to say, His Excellency may call into council others besides privy councillors, and then swear them in but in this case it was his right to call in certain persons. He called on the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, then leader of the opposition, to form a government. That was one call. Certain other privy councillors already
[Mr. Stevens.J
sworn in were then called into council for the purpose of doing the very things which constitutionally it was proper for a privy councillor to do. The outcome of that is the present government, admittedly carrying on temporarily, frankly so stated to the House and well known and thoroughly understood by the country. We are merely asking that the business of a session admittedly drawing to a close, most of which-
Just beginning.

I am really serious in
this, and I do not wish to burlesque it. I say this long, arduous, tedious session is admittedly drawing to a close; the business is completed with the exception of one or two non-contentious bills and a portion of the estimates. We say this:	We are ready to
accept the estimates as already prepared; we will carry out the mandate of the House in the expenditure of these moneys with one reservation, that we purpose to be as economical as possible in the administration of these estimates, and we will try to bring the business of the House to a close. That is all we are asking at present. I admit that it is quite within the right of hon. gentlemen opposite, and quite within the right of my right hon. friend, to challenge the government whenever they see fit. But I do call into question the logic or fairness of his argument when he seeks to lead the House to believe that there was something unconstitutional in the act either of His Excellency or of the present Prime Minister.
I have a right to reply, I think.
I have the floor, I believe

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Did you wish to ask a question?

I wanted to
reply to a point raised by my hon. friend.

I am only going to take a
few moments. The right hon. leader of the opposition has detailed to us the circumstances under which he offered the resignation of himself and his colleagues to His Excellency the Governor General, and he has stated very clearly that in offering his resignation he did not advise His Excellency to call upon any member of this House to form an administration. The reason he did not so advise His Excellency was that he did not believe any member of this House to be competent to fill that high office, with the exception of himself. He left His Excellency the Governor General without advice; he left the country without a government except as
