represented by His Excellency the Governor General. There may be no interregnum in the government of a country such as this, with a constitution such as we possess, and therefore His Excellency had to exercise his own discretion in calling upon a member of this House to form an administration, and, in the exercise of that discretion, he called upon the then leader of the opposition.
Now, what are the prerogatives of His Excellency, and who are to advise him under the constitution of the country? I read section 11 of the British North America Act, and I cite it now so that hon. gentlemen may give it their attention before we again meet to-morrow. Section 11 says:
There shall be a council to aid and advise the government of Canada, to be styled the Queen's Privy Council for Canada; and the persons who are to be members of that council shall be from time to time chosen and summoned by the Governor General and sworn in as Privy Councillors, and members thereof may be from time to time removed by the Governor General.
Therefore the Governor General, left without advice, even if there were no privy councillor living in Canada, would have the right to appoint privy councillors to advise him, but he also had the right to ask any existing ,privy councillors to come in and advise him in a crisis such as confronted him when the then Prime Minister of this country tendered his resignation and insisted upon its immediate acceptance.
May I ask a question?

I am not answering questions just now. Then section 12 of the British North America Act provides:
All powers, authorities and functions which under any act of the parliament of Great Britain, or of the parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, oc of the legislature of Upper Canada, Lower Canada, Canada, Nova Scotia or New Brunswick, are at the Union vested in or exerciseable by the respective Governors or Lieutenant-Governors of those provinces, with the advice, or with the advice and consent, of the respective executive councils thereof, or in conjunction with those councils, or with any number of members thereof, or by -those Governors or Lieutenant-Governors individually, shall, as far as the same con-hinue in existence and capable of being exercised after the Union in relation to the government of Canada, be vested in and exerciseable by the Governor General, with the advice or with the advice and consent of or in conjunction with the Queen's Privy Council for Canada, or any members thereof, or by the Governor-General individually, as the case requires. . .
So if some calamity had wiped out every privy councillor in Canada or had taken away the life of every member of the existing cabinet, under this constitution His Excellency had the right there and then to appoint new privy councillors, if he saw fit, to assemble
and advise him in such a crisis, in order that the country might not be left without a government. But according to the statement made here to-night, His Excellency, being left without official advisers, by reason of the resignation of the present right hon. leader of the opposition, called in a certain number -I do not know how many-of privy councillors, who had previously taken the oath of office and who had continued to be members of the Privy Council, and asked for their advice. He also had with him the present Prime Minister, who is not now a member of this House, whom he had selected and appointed as Prime Minister, and who had. been nominated to occupy the portfolios of Minister of External Affairs and President of the Privy Council. The Governor General had a perfect right to take the advice of the Prime Minister, whom he had selected, as to what members of the Privy Council of Canada, who are numerous, should be called in to form a committee of the Privy Council for the purpose of attending to these matters of administration which demanded immediate attention. So they assembled and proceeded correctly under the constitution, and there was no other alternative than to take the measures which were taken by them to give the country a temporary government. The right hon. leader of the opposition disclosed by his speech to-night, and it is a fair criticism to say that he desired to force this parliament into dissolution, that he took the means that he did at the time in order to force a dissolution of parliament, which His Excellency in the exercise of his discretion refused to grant to him.
I am told that my hon. friend said I had refused to carry on.

I was not discussing that at
present.

speechtext: I think the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, while perhaps not exactly out of order, certainly went a little bit too far in the implication which was contained in his statement, and in order to maintain decorum of debate I would ask him to withdraw that expression.

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman, and I withdraw it. I am perfectly willing, if in the heat of debate I go beyond the proper line, to apologize to the Chairman and to the committee. What I was about to say is this, that the former Prime Minister, the present leader of the opposition, handed in his resignation under very peculiar circumstances, circumstances unprecedented, except for one occasion in the history of this country. He had challenged this House on the matter of the Customs report, but he avoided a direct and final vote upon the amendment offered to that report, which amendment he was opposing. He lost confidence in himself and felt, no doubt, that he could not further command the support and confidence of this House. Before that report and' the 'Stevens amendment to it, which reflected upon the then Prime Minister and his administration, could come before this House for final decision, his courage oozed out at his finger tips or at his toes- I do not know which-and he rushed off to tender his resignation to the Governor General.
I did not rush. I went down on Saturday, and we discussed the matter calmly from Saturday until Monday.
I suppose he did discuss it, but anyway the final rush I think was made somewhere about twelve o'clock noon on Monday.

The final meeting with His Excellency was on Monday by appointment which had been made on the Sunday previous, the appointment being so arranged in order that His Excellency might take whatever steps he desired to take with reference to accepting my resignation at that time.
Mr. 'CAHAN: Whether the resignation was tendered on Saturday or on the following Monday, and accepted' then, the obvious object of the advice given by the Prime Minister at that time for a dissolution of this parliament was to prevent this parliament from exercising its duty and its responsibility of passing upon the conduct of the late administration in connection with the Customs report.
I deny that statement absolutely.

The circumstances under
which, admittedly, the Prime Minister on Saturday or on Monday offered his resignation convey that fair inference, because, in

the very act of advising a dissolution, if he really desired a dissolution, he knew that, if dissolution were granted, it would prevent this House from passing the reprimand upon himself and his administration which was contained in the amendments to the Customs report.

May I say to my hon. friend that I have the strongest reasons not only for believing but for knowing that the so-called censure that he talks about would never have been passed on this government had this government remained in office until after that vote was taken, and that vote was only passed because of this co-operation between a certain number of gentlemen to my left and hon. gentleman *opposite to prevent a dissolution of this parliament.

I can only infer, and members of this House can only infer, as the leader of the opposition himself infers, what would have taken place if the resolution of censure contained in the Stevens amendment had been allowed by the. late government to foe voted upon by this House. But when _ the advice of the right hon. gentleman was tendered to His Excellency for a dissolution and refused, as we believe, in the exercise of :a constitutional right, within the discretion of His Excellency the Governor General, this country was left without a government, and 1 suggest that the proper procedure was taken *in selecting a prime minister and in summoning a certain number of the king's privy councillors in Canada to advise during the interregnum, while the new Prime Minister was forming his cabinet, and that there is nothing -exceptional in any member of the King's Privy Council being appointed by a committee of that Privy Council to be acting minister, for the time being, of any department. Nay, more than that, as there will be a recess, I will venture to say that the leader of the opposition to-night, if he searches the records of his own administration, will find more than a single instance in which a member of the upper house-I refer to Senator Dandu-rand, a member of his own government-
My hon. friend is beginning to talk about the Senate.

Well, Senator Dandurand
was a member of the previous government without portfolio, but he held and exercised various administrative offices in the government of the right hon. gentleman, although he was never sworn in or took the oath as minister of any special department.

My hon. friend does not get my point. I never for a moment denied that you could have acting ministers. But what I do say is this: You have got to have a ministry constituted in the first instance of ministers who are sworn in and able to carry on business, and who, after they are sworn in, go back to the people for re-election.
Oh, well!

After you have gone through the process and got the ministry duly formed in accordance with the constitutional practice in respect to the taking of office, then if you want to add one or two ministers as acting ministers to take the place of a minister who has become too old or, as my hon. friend says, take a portfolio which has been vacated by death, you can do so; but it, was never contemplated by any constitution under heaven that a ministry should be composed entirely of acting ministers. That is reducing the matter to the reductio ad absur-dum.
My reply to that is that it is never-

I venture to say that my hon. friend will never be able to quote a precedent in British history where a minister pretending to administer a department of government ever came into parliament while parliament was in session without having resigned his office of emolument under the crown in order to go back to the people for re-election. If he takes an office of emolument he must obtain the approval of the people. A minister of the crown is not in the same position as a private member. When a member of parliament takes office under the crown he is then in an entirely different position in relation to the electorate. He has got to go back to the people and receive endorsa-tion, and if he does not get that endorsation he is not able :to act as a member of the ministry.

Rather than meet the House and allow the House to give its verdict on that report, he advised the dissolution of parliament, which he knew would prevent the House from passing judgment on that report. He thereby placed the country in a most peculiar and unprecedented position which rendered it absolutely necessary that His Excellency the Governor General, in accordance with the

constitution, should ask the members of the privy council to come and advise him. They did assemble and did advise him, and, acting within their prerogatives as a committee of the privy council, they appointed certain members of parliament to act temporarily in the administration of the several offices to which they were then designated. That procedure is constitutional. Precedents have been established time after time during the ministry of the right hon. leader of the opposition with respect to one, two and sometimes three members of the government.

If my hon.
friend wishes to make precedents, may I say that no acting minister was appointed during the entire period of my administration until the government had sworn ministers who had to go back to the people for re-election, ministers who had undertaken the duty of carrying on the business of the country.
That is merely a facetious explanation-
Oh, no.

-because the right hon.
gentleman has admitted that he had called in members of the Privy Council who did temporarily administer the affairs of particular departments without taking a new oath of office at all, it being well known that their appointments and oaths as privy councillors qualified them to receive temporary nominations for the administration of the particular offices to which they were temporarily appointed by order in council. The right hon. gentleman brought about an unprecedented condition of affairs in this country. 1 will not reflect further upon his motives in bringing about that condition of affairs, which had to be met by exceptional measures; but he will look in vain to find any precedent established from which it can be shown or from which it can be adduced that anything irregular or unconstitutional has taken place in the recent formation of what he now calls *"a shadow ministry."
